title: Read a solicitation
subtitle: Guide · Section L.2
summary: How a federal solicitation is laid out, which sections to read first and what to find before you decide to bid.
content: Read a solicitation How a federal solicitation is laid out, which sections to read first and what to find before you decide to bid. field L.2   A solicitation is the government’s written request for offers. It can run to hundreds of pages, and most of those pages are not where the decisions are. This guide explains how the document is organized so you can find the dozen facts that tell you whether to bid, and what a winning answer has to contain. The kinds of request Not everything the government posts is a solicitation, and the different kinds are answered differently. | Name | What it is | What you send back | | --- | --- | --- | | Request for information (RFI) or sources sought | Market research. The government is learning who can

title: The kinds of request
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: Not everything the government posts is a solicitation, and the different kinds are answered differently. | Name | What it is | What you send back | | --- | --- ...
content: The kinds of request Read a solicitation Not everything the government posts is a solicitation, and the different kinds are answered differently. | Name | What it is | What you send back | | --- | --- | --- | | Request for information (RFI) or sources sought | Market research. The government is learning who can do the work | A short description of your capability. It is not an offer and cannot win a contract | | Draft solicitation | An early version, posted for comment | Questions and comments | | Request for quotation (RFQ) | A request for prices, common for smaller and simpler buys | A quote | | Request for proposals (RFP) | The full process for negotiated contracts, with instructions and evaluation factors | A proposal, usually in several volumes | | Invitation for bids (IFB) | Sealed bidding. The award goes on price to a responsive, responsible bidder | A bid | Federal opportunities above a set dollar value are posted on SAM.gov under Contract Opportunities. Searching and reading there is free and needs no account. Downloading some attachments does need one. An RFI is worth answering. The answers help the government decide whether a purchase can be set aside for small businesses, and how to write the requirement.

title: The lettered sections
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: Many solicitations follow the uniform contract format, which divides the document into thirteen lettered sections. Even when a solicitation is laid out differen...
content: The lettered sections Read a solicitation Many solicitations follow the uniform contract format, which divides the document into thirteen lettered sections. Even when a solicitation is laid out differently, people in this field use the letters as shorthand, so they are worth learning once. | Section | Title | What you find there | | --- | --- | --- | | A | Solicitation/contract form | The cover form: solicitation number, issuing office, due date and time | | B | Supplies or services and prices/costs | The line items you will price | | C | Description/specifications/statement of work | The work | | D | Packaging and marking | How deliverables are packed and labeled | | E | Inspection and acceptance | How and where the government accepts the work | | F | Deliveries or performance | Dates, period of performance, place | | G | Contract administration data | Who administers the contract, and how to invoice | | H | Special contract requirements | Terms particular to this contract: security, key personnel, transitions | | I | Contract clauses | The standard clauses, mostly by reference | | J | List of attachments | Everything attached, by title | | K | Representations, certifications and other statements | Statements you make about your company | | L | Instructions, conditions and notices to offerors | How to prepare and submit the proposal | | M | Evaluation factors for award | How the proposal will be judged | Sections A through J become the contract. Section K is carried into it by reference. Sections L and M are about the competition, and are not part of the contract. The Federal Acquisition Regulation is being rewritten. For decades the uniform contract format has been at FAR 15.204-1, and it is still there in the codified text. The overhaul text that agencies have been working from since 2025 moves it to a different section and makes it optional. Expect to see both layouts for some time, and find the rule by its title on acquisition.gov instead of trusting a section number from memory, including the ones in this guide.

title: When the letters are missing
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: Purchases of commercial products and services often use a shorter layout, built around a standard form and a set of commercial clauses. There may be no Section ...
content: When the letters are missing Read a solicitation Purchases of commercial products and services often use a shorter layout, built around a standard form and a set of commercial clauses. There may be no Section L or M by name. The same content is still there under plainer headings: - Instructions to offerors is the equivalent of Section L. - Evaluation or basis for award is the equivalent of Section M. - Statement of work , performance work statement or statement of objectives is the equivalent of Section C. - Price schedule is the equivalent of Section B. Other transaction agreements, which some defense buyers use for prototypes, are not governed by the FAR at all. Their requests follow whatever format the issuing office chooses. Read them without assumptions.

title: What to read first
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: Reading from page one is the slow way. This order gets you to a bid decision fastest: 1. The cover page. Due date, time and time zone. How to submit. Who to ask...
content: What to read first Read a solicitation Reading from page one is the slow way. This order gets you to a bid decision fastest: 1. The cover page. Due date, time and time zone. How to submit. Who to ask. 2. Section L. What you must hand in: volumes, page limits, format, required forms. 3. Section M. What the government will score, and what matters most. 4. Section C. The work itself. Can you do it? 5. Section B. How the price is structured. 6. Section H. Anything unusual: clearances, key personnel, special security terms. 7. Sections I and K. The clauses and the statements you must make. 8. Section J attachments. Often the real detail lives here: the pricing workbook, the labor category descriptions, the data requirements.

title: The first-pass list
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: Before you spend a day on a solicitation, find these facts. Most are on the cover page or in Sections L and M. - Deadlines. When questions are due. When the pro...
content: The first-pass list Read a solicitation Before you spend a day on a solicitation, find these facts. Most are on the cover page or in Sections L and M. - Deadlines. When questions are due. When the proposal is due, to the minute, and in which time zone. - How to submit. A portal, email, or something else, and any size limit on files. - Who may bid. Whether the purchase is set aside for small businesses or a specific program, and under which NAICS code and size standard. See Codes, registration and small business status. - Contract type. Fixed price, time and materials, cost reimbursement, or an ordering contract with task orders. - Length. The base period and the option periods. - Place of performance. On a government site, at your own, or remote. - Security. Whether people or facilities need a clearance, and how government information must be protected. See Protecting government information. - Basis for award. Whether the government will trade price against quality, or take the lowest-priced proposal that is technically acceptable. - Past performance. How many references, how recent and how similar. - Mandatory qualifications. Certifications, registrations or experience that are pass or fail. If you fail a pass-or-fail item, nothing else in the proposal matters.

title: Clauses incorporated by reference
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: Section I can list a hundred clauses by number and title alone. Each one is a term of the contract, with the same force as if it were printed in full. The full ...
content: Clauses incorporated by reference Read a solicitation Section I can list a hundred clauses by number and title alone. Each one is a term of the contract, with the same force as if it were printed in full. The full text is on acquisition.gov. The numbers tell you where a clause comes from: | Pattern | Source | | --- | --- | | 52.2xx-xx | The Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) | | 252.2xx-7xxx | The Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) | | Other prefixes | Another agency’s supplement | You do not need to read every clause on the first pass. These are worth finding early, because they change what the work costs: | Subject | Long-standing clause | Why it matters | | --- | --- | --- | | Safeguarding contractor systems | FAR 52.204-21 | Fifteen basic security requirements for any system holding federal contract information | | Safeguarding defense information | DFARS 252.204-7012 | NIST SP 800-171 and 72-hour incident reporting | | CMMC | DFARS 252.204-7021 | A required CMMC level | | Limitations on subcontracting | FAR 52.219-14 | How much of a set-aside contract you must perform yourself | | Service contract labor standards | FAR 52.222-41 | Minimum wages and benefits for covered service workers | | Prompt payment | FAR 52.232-25 | When you are paid, and interest if you are not | Some of these are being renumbered as part of the rewrite described above. Search by the clause title if a number does not match.

title: Amendments and questions
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: A solicitation changes after it is posted. Each change is an amendment, and each one is part of the solicitation. - Watch for amendments. On SAM.gov you can fol...
content: Amendments and questions Read a solicitation A solicitation changes after it is posted. Each change is an amendment, and each one is part of the solicitation. - Watch for amendments. On SAM.gov you can follow an opportunity. An amendment can move the due date, change the work or replace an attachment. - Acknowledge every amendment in the way the solicitation requires. A proposal that ignores an amendment can be rejected. - Ask questions in writing, by the deadline, to the person named. Answers are normally published to every bidder, so do not put anything proprietary in a question. - Do not rely on anything said informally. Only the written solicitation and its amendments count. A good question points to a page and paragraph, quotes the text and asks one thing.

title: Late is late
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: A proposal that arrives after the exact time stated is late, and with narrow exceptions a late proposal is not considered. Portals slow down in the last hour, a...
content: Late is late Read a solicitation A proposal that arrives after the exact time stated is late, and with narrow exceptions a late proposal is not considered. Portals slow down in the last hour, and email attachments are held up by size limits and scanners. Plan to submit a day early.

title: Decide whether to bid
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: A proposal costs real time. Before you commit, answer these honestly: - Are we eligible, and do we pass every pass-or-fail item? - Can we do the work in Section...
content: Decide whether to bid Read a solicitation A proposal costs real time. Before you commit, answer these honestly: - Are we eligible, and do we pass every pass-or-fail item? - Can we do the work in Section C with people we have or can hire? - Do we have past performance that matches what Section M asks for? - Can we meet the security requirements by the time they apply? - Does the price structure in Section B leave room to do the work properly? - Can we produce everything Section L asks for by the due date? Deciding not to bid is a legitimate result of reading a solicitation well. When the answer is yes, the next guide covers answering every requirement.

content: Request a tool Request a tool or add your own A useful request covers three things: - The job. What you need to produce, and what you do by hand today. “I rebuild a spreadsheet that turns our pools into rates for every proposal” is a job. “A pricing tool” is not. - Who needs it. For example, a solo developer pricing a first bid, or a small company preparing for a first assessment. - The public source. The regulation, standard or guide the tool would be based on, with a link if you have one. You can copy this outline into an issue or an email: The last line matters more than it looks. If a tool would be useless to you the moment it asked for a company name, say so. What happens to a suggestion A suggestion is treated the same way as any other idea for a tool: How we decide what to build has the gates and the rubric in full.

title: Add a tool you built
subtitle: Request a tool or add your own
summary: Tools live in their own repositories, under your own name or organization. ClearedStack lists them. It does not take them over. To be listed, a tool has to be: ...
content: Add a tool you built Request a tool or add your own Tools live in their own repositories, under your own name or organization. ClearedStack lists them. It does not take them over. To be listed, a tool has to be: 1. Free and open source , under an OSI-approved license, with no paid tier and no ads. 2. Client-side. It runs in the browser or on the user’s own machine, and does not send what the user enters to any server. 3. Free of tracking : no analytics, no third-party scripts, no accounts. 4. Built from public sources , and clear about which ones. 5. Honest about its limits , including that its output is not professional advice. To list it: 1. Fork this site’s repository. 2. Add one entry to src/data/catalog.ts . 3. Open a pull request that links to your tool and its repository. The entry looks like this: The home page, the catalog, the tool’s own page and every count are generated from that file, so the one entry is the whole change. An entry can also carry an optional provenance field that records where the idea came from. Work on this site lists every field, and Build a tool that can be listed goes through each condition in detail, with a checklist to run before you open the pull request.

title: How a listing is reviewed
subtitle: Request a tool or add your own
summary: A person reads the pull request and uses the tool. The review checks the five conditions and nothing else: - the license file is there - the Network tab stays q...
content: How a listing is reviewed Request a tool or add your own A person reads the pull request and uses the tool. The review checks the five conditions and nothing else: - the license file is there - the Network tab stays quiet while the tool is used, and the tool still works with the network disconnected - the page loads nothing from other companies’ servers - the README names the sources and says what the tool does not cover - the examples and test data are made up The review does not certify that every result is correct. That is why each tool has to name its sources: so that anyone can check. A tool that later breaks a condition is taken off the list until it is fixed.

title: What never goes in
subtitle: Request a tool or add your own
summary: Do not put any of these in a request, an issue, an email, a pull request, a tool or its test data: - classified information - controlled unclassified informatio...
content: What never goes in Request a tool or add your own Do not put any of these in a request, an issue, an email, a pull request, a tool or its test data: - classified information - controlled unclassified information (CUI) - export-controlled technical data - real contract data, real rates, or anything that identifies a real company’s bid - text copied from a solicitation that is not publicly posted “Public” means officially released. A document that leaked, or that is marked for limited distribution but can be found online anyway, is not public for this project. If you are unsure, leave it out and describe the problem in your own words with made-up numbers.

content: Work on this site Set the site up on your own machine, find your way around the code, add a guide, a platform page or a catalog entry, and send the change. contribute L.4   The site you are reading is one small repository. Fixing a typo, correcting a guide and adding a tool to the catalog are all changes to a text file in it. This guide shows where everything is. What the site is made of The site is built with Next.js, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS, and exported as static files. It has no server, no API routes and no database. The guides are written in MDX, which is Markdown that can also hold a few components. You do not need to know any of those to fix a sentence. You need a text editor and a GitHub account. Make a small fix without installing anything For a typo

content: Add or change a catalog entry Work on this site Open src/data/catalog.ts and add an entry to the tools list: | Field | What to put there | | --- | --- | | slug | A short name in lowercase with hyphens. It must be unique | | name | The tool’s name as people will read it | | summary | One sentence that starts with a verb and says what the tool produces | | category | One of pricing , proposal , cyber , market , devsecops | | status | planned , building or live | | url | Where the tool runs. Add it when the tool is live | | repo | The source repository. Add it when the repository is public | The home page, the catalog page and every count on them are generated from this list. There is nothing else to update. Each tool also gets a page of its own at /tools// . These optional fields fill it in: | Field | What to put there | | --- | --- | | detail | Two or three sentences on what the tool does | | inputs | A list of what the user brings to it | | outputs | A list of what the user leaves with | | sources | The public sources it is built from, each with a name and, where there is one, a url | | guides | The guides that explain the subject: a slug , and optionally the section heading to open at | | provenance | Where the idea came from, if another tool or document inspired it | The build stops with a message if a tool names a guide or a heading that does not exist. A tool can also have a detailed specification: the inputs, the logic, the checks and the worked examples it is tested against. Put it in src/tools/.mdx , named after the tool’s slug , and it is shown on the tool’s page under the summary.

title: What you can use in a guide
subtitle: Work on this site
summary: Ordinary Markdown works: headings, bold text, links, numbered and bulleted lists, code blocks and tables. - Second-level headings ( ) become the table of conten...
content: What you can use in a guide Work on this site Ordinary Markdown works: headings, bold text, links, numbered and bulleted lists, code blocks and tables. - Second-level headings ( ) become the table of contents and get a link of their own. Keep them short, and do not repeat one within a guide. - Links to other pages on the site start with a slash, such as /guides/your-data/ . - Tables use pipes. Put ---: under a column to align numbers to the right. - Callouts set a short passage apart: The kind can be note , check or warning . Use them sparingly. A page with five callouts has none. Two characters need care in MDX, because it reads them as code: a left curly brace and a less-than sign. Write “less than” in words, or put the text in backticks.

content: How the guides are written Work on this site The guides are for people who are good at their own work and new to this subject. A few habits keep them readable: - Plain words. If a simpler word says the same thing, use it. - Define a term the first time it appears , and add it to the glossary. - One idea per paragraph. Short sentences. - Say what to do , then why. - Cite the rule. Name the regulation and the part, so the reader can check. - Date anything that changes. Do not print a rate or a threshold without saying when it was current, or better, tell the reader where to look it up. - Made-up examples only. No real companies, contracts or rates. Guides that describe regulations should set reviewed and end with a “Sources” section.

title: What happens to what you type
subtitle: Guide · Section L.1
summary: Where your information goes when you use the site or a tool, what can still see it, and how to confirm all of it yourself.
content: What happens to what you type Where your information goes when you use the site or a tool, what can still see it, and how to confirm all of it yourself. start L.1   The short answer is that it stays on your computer. This guide explains what that means, where the limits are, and how to check it without taking anyone’s word for it. What “runs in your browser” means Most web applications work in two halves. The page in front of you collects what you type and sends it to a server, the server does the work, and the answer comes back. Your information has left your computer by the time you see a result. The tools listed here have only the first half. When you open one, your browser downloads the page and its code once. After that, the arithmetic, the text pars

title: What “runs in your browser” means
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: Most web applications work in two halves. The page in front of you collects what you type and sends it to a server, the server does the work, and the answer com...
content: What “runs in your browser” means What happens to what you type Most web applications work in two halves. The page in front of you collects what you type and sends it to a server, the server does the work, and the answer comes back. Your information has left your computer by the time you see a result. The tools listed here have only the first half. When you open one, your browser downloads the page and its code once. After that, the arithmetic, the text parsing and the file reading are all done by that code on your machine. There is no server waiting for your input, because the project does not run one. That is also why the tools cost nothing to run and need no account. There is nothing on the other end to pay for or to sign in to.

title: No AI in the tools

content: No AI in the tools What happens to what you type A tool contains no AI model and makes no call to one. Its calculations and parsers are ordinary code that you can read in the tool’s public repository, and the same input gives the same answer every time. AI assistants are used only while the code and the guides are being written, to help one human maintainer draft them. A person checks every fact and formula against the official text before it is released. See How AI is used to build this project.

title: This website
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: clearedstack.com is a set of plain files. It has: - no accounts and no sign-in - no cookies - no analytics or visitor counting - no fonts, scripts or images loa...
content: This website What happens to what you type clearedstack.com is a set of plain files. It has: - no accounts and no sign-in - no cookies - no analytics or visitor counting - no fonts, scripts or images loaded from other companies’ servers The last point is enforced, not just promised. Every page carries a content security policy, which is an instruction to your browser. This site’s policy says that scripts, styles, fonts and images may load only from the site itself, that the page may connect only to the site itself, and that forms may not be submitted anywhere. If a line of code tried to send something elsewhere, your browser would refuse.

title: What a web server always sees

content: What a web server always sees What happens to what you type One limit applies to every website, this one included. To send you a page, the server has to know where to send it. So the company that hosts the files can see: - the IP address the request came from - which page was asked for, and when - the browser name your browser reports Nothing you type into a tool is part of that. If even this is more than your situation allows, run a copy inside your own network. See Host your own copy.

title: Check it yourself
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: You can confirm that a tool keeps your input on your machine in about a minute. Use made-up numbers for the test. 1. Open the tool. 2. Open your browser’s devel...
content: Check it yourself What happens to what you type You can confirm that a tool keeps your input on your machine in about a minute. Use made-up numbers for the test. 1. Open the tool. 2. Open your browser’s developer tools. Press F12 on Windows or Linux, or Command-Option-I on a Mac. 3. Choose the Network tab. It lists every request the page makes. 4. Clear the list. There is a clear button at the top left of the panel. 5. Use the tool as you normally would. Type numbers, paste text, load a file. 6. Watch the list. A tool that works on your machine adds nothing to the list while you type. If a request does appear, click it and look at what was sent. A request that carries what you entered is a failure of the listing rules, and the project wants to hear about it. A second check needs no developer tools. Load the tool, then disconnect from the network: turn off Wi-Fi or unplug the cable. Keep using the tool. If it still gives answers, the work is happening on your computer.

content: Read the policy What happens to what you type To see the content security policy for yourself: 1. Open any page on this site. 2. Right-click and choose View Page Source . 3. Search for Content-Security-Policy . You will find a line listing what the page is allowed to load and where it is allowed to connect. connect-src 'self' is the part that stops a page from sending data to another server. The same test works on any tool. A tool with no such policy is not necessarily sending anything, but one that has it gives you a stronger guarantee than a promise.

title: What can still see your screen
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: Keeping data off a server does not make it invisible. Everything below runs on your side, outside any website’s control: - Browser extensions. Many extensions c...
content: What can still see your screen What happens to what you type Keeping data off a server does not make it invisible. Everything below runs on your side, outside any website’s control: - Browser extensions. Many extensions can read every page you open. A grammar checker, a password manager or a shopping helper may see what you type. For sensitive work, use a browser profile with no extensions or a private window with extensions turned off. - Company monitoring. A work computer may record screens, keystrokes or web traffic. That is your employer’s system and their rules apply. - Clipboard tools. If you copy a rate out of a tool, a clipboard manager or a cloud clipboard may keep it. - Screen sharing. A tool open in a shared window is visible to the meeting. - Translation and “AI assistant” features built into a browser may send page text to a service. Turn them off for the tab, or use a browser without them.

title: Saved work on a shared computer
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: A tool may let you keep your work between visits by saving it in the browser’s own storage. That storage is on your computer and is not sent anywhere. It does m...
content: Saved work on a shared computer What happens to what you type A tool may let you keep your work between visits by saving it in the browser’s own storage. That storage is on your computer and is not sent anywhere. It does mean the next person to use the same browser profile can open the tool and see what you left. On a shared or borrowed computer: - use a private window, which discards its storage when you close it, or - clear the site’s data when you finish, from your browser’s privacy settings. Files you export from a tool are ordinary files. Store and send them the way you would any other document with the same contents.

title: What not to enter
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: - Classified information : never. No tool listed here is approved for it, and neither is an ordinary web browser. - Controlled unclassified information (CUI) : ...
content: What not to enter What happens to what you type - Classified information : never. No tool listed here is approved for it, and neither is an ordinary web browser. - Controlled unclassified information (CUI) : running in a browser does not change the rules for the computer you are sitting at. Handle CUI only on a system your contract and your company’s policy allow. If that system cannot reach the internet, host a copy of the tool on it. - Export-controlled technical data : the same reasoning applies. The tool does not send it anywhere, but your obligations attach to the machine and the people who can see it. - Proprietary rates and bid data : this is yours to decide. Nothing leaves your machine, so the question is the one above: who else can see your screen and your browser. If you are unsure whether something is safe to enter, use made-up numbers first to learn how the tool behaves.

title: Interfaces & State Transitions
subtitle: Assay specification
summary: Assay polls Muster in the clearedstack namespace over ServiceAccount-authenticated cluster-private HTTP ( CONTRACT VERSION=v1 ), draining urgent → normal → back...
content: Interfaces & State Transitions Assay specification Assay polls Muster in the clearedstack namespace over ServiceAccount-authenticated cluster-private HTTP ( CONTRACT VERSION=v1 ), draining urgent → normal → backfill lanes. - Inbound state: observed (structured JSON facts produced by Sextant). - Evaluation stages: 1. Five binary knockout gates: - Public source — Rules, formulas, and thresholds must come from officially released public materials (statutes, FAR, DFARS, NIST SPs). - Runs in the browser — Must execute entirely client-side (HTML/CSS/JS/WASM) with no backend server or remote API. - Private by design — Must work offline, require no accounts, emit zero tracking, and enforce connect-src 'self' . - One job — Must perform a single focused task describable in one active verb-first sentence. - Arithmetic, not advice — Must compute numbers, structure data, or look up citations—never render legal advice. 2. 100-point rubric: Candidates clearing all five gates are rated 1 – 5 across seven weighted factors (composite 20 – 100 ): Need for small businesses ( ×4 , 20 pts), Gap ( ×4 , 20 pts), Strength of public source ( ×3 , 15 pts), Fits in a browser ( ×3 , 15 pts), Small enough to read ( ×2 , 10 pts), Can be checked ( ×2 , 10 pts), and Low upkeep of reference data ( ×2 , 10 pts). 3. Preliminary recommendation & split/merge flag: Assigns Build (Score ≥ 75 and Gap > 1), Link (Score ≥ 75 and Gap = 1), Park (Score 55–74), or Reject (Score < 55). Flags split/merge review when Need is 4 – 5 and Small enough to read is 1 – 2 . 4. Five deterministic tie-breakers: Roadmap phase fit → Gap severity → Low upkeep → Small code footprint → Community demand. - Outbound transitions: - screened-out — Candidate failed one or more knockout gates (failure reason logged publicly). - scored — Candidate cleared all five gates and received its rubric breakdown and recommendation. - needs subtool — Fail-closed pause ( E NEEDS SUBTOOL ) when an item's category lacks a matching rubric profile.

content: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries Assay specification - Zero raw observation access: Assay operates strictly on sanitized structured JSON facts from observed records; it never reads raw vendor HTML, screenshots, or binary PDFs. - Public transparency: All knockout gate outcomes, rubric weights, factor scores, and tie-breaker results are written through Muster to core. and exposed read-only via pub. views on clearedstack.com with no login wall. - Pod hardening & network policy: Runs as an unprivileged non-root container with dropped capabilities, read-only root filesystem (writable only at /var/spool/cs ), zero database credentials, and default-deny NetworkPolicy permitting only ServiceAccount HTTP to Muster.

content: Interfaces & State Transitions Bellbuoy specification Bellbuoy pulls leased notification and routing jobs from Muster over cluster-private HTTP using its Kubernetes ServiceAccount identity ( lease , heartbeat , complete , fail , needs subtool ), always draining urgent before normal and normal before backfill . It never connects directly to Logbook. Rather than transitioning PA-XXXX items through pipeline stages itself, Bellbuoy reacts to pipeline events and Countersign approvals: - Deterministic issue deduplication: Computes a repeatable fingerprint from the worker name, sanitized error code ( E TIMEOUT , E PARSE , E NEEDS SUBTOOL ), and failure pattern. If an open issue with that fingerprint already exists in Plainforge, Bellbuoy increments its occurrence count instead of creating duplicate tickets. - Edit-to-repo loop ( ownership map.json ): Routes owner-approved anonymous ✎ Edit proposals ( DATA , CONFIG , ISSUE from Countersign)—committing CONFIG branches/PRs or ISSUE tickets to Plainforge so Keelworks can build/test and Shipkeeper can deploy. - Live Portal SSE: Streams sanitized status updates so an anonymous visitor watches their edit pill move live from Proposed → Approved → Building → Live .

title: Why nothing that runs uses AI
subtitle: How AI is used to build this project
summary: Many pipelines call a model whenever they meet an unfamiliar page, an awkward table or a messy edge case. This design does the opposite. When a worker meets som...
content: Why nothing that runs uses AI How AI is used to build this project Many pipelines call a model whenever they meet an unfamiliar page, an awkward table or a messy edge case. This design does the opposite. When a worker meets something it has no rule for, it stops work on that item and asks for a rule. The rule is then written, with AI help if that is useful, reviewed by the owner, tested against saved examples and deployed. From then on that case is handled by code. The difference is that every solved case becomes something permanent and checkable, instead of a guess that might come out differently next time. In federal contracting a guess is worse than a gap.

summary: What is taken from an existing tool and what never is, how the wall between looking and building is kept, how ideas are credited, and how a vendor can ask for a correction.
content: Clean room and credit What is taken from an existing tool and what never is, how the wall between looking and building is kept, how ideas are credited, and how a vendor can ask for a correction. factory J.1 design  Federal regulations belong to everyone. A piece of software that implements one belongs to its author. ClearedStack takes ideas for tools from products that already exist, so it has to be exact about the difference: it takes the job to be done and nothing else. This page describes that rule, how the pipeline is designed to enforce it, and how the source of an idea is credited. Build, link or skip The first question is whether to build at all. If a free tool already runs on the user’s machine, respects privacy and cites public sources, rebuilding it is wasted effort. What is taken and what is n

content: What is taken and what is not Clean room and credit Open-source libraries under permissive licenses (MIT, BSD, Apache 2.0) may be used inside a tool, with their copyright notices and license files kept. Code under a strong copyleft license is not mixed into the project’s MIT repositories. A good copyleft tool is linked to instead.

content: The wall between looking and building Clean room and credit The rule is not left to good intentions. The worker that looks and the worker that builds are separate programs in separate repositories, and what passes between them is controlled. | Stage | What it can see | What it passes on | | --- | --- | --- | | Sextant | Public pages and documents | A structured record of facts. The page itself is sealed and goes no further | | Assay, Countersign | The record and the scores | A decision: link, build, park or reject | | Waybill | The official rule and its worked examples | A specification with no vendor material in it | | Moldloft | Only the specification and its own templates | A new tool, built without ever seeing the product that inspired it | Because the builder never receives the observed page, it cannot echo its layout, its wording or its code.

content: The specification Clean room and credit The specification is the only thing that crosses the wall. It has four parts. | Part | What goes in | What is left out | | --- | --- | --- | | Provenance | The credit note, the date observed and whether the vendor has opted out | The captured pages, and vendor marketing links | | Authority | The official citations and their effective dates | Any vendor reading that conflicts with the government text | | Schema | The inputs, outputs, units, limits and formulas | Vendor field labels and internal structure | | Examples | Public worked examples and boundary cases | Any test data taken from a vendor | Where a commercial tool gives an answer that conflicts with an official publication, the specification follows the official publication.

title: How an idea is credited
subtitle: Clean room and credit
summary: A tool inspired by an existing product carries a short note in a fixed form, so the wording never varies and never editorializes. Idea seen in : the product and...
content: How an idea is credited Clean room and credit A tool inspired by an existing product carries a short note in a fixed form, so the wording never varies and never editorializes. Idea seen in : the product and its maker, and the month its public pages were looked at. What we took : the job, in one sentence. What we did differently : runs in your browser, free, no account, built from the named regulation. Four rules apply to every note: - It records only that a workflow was seen on a public page on a given date. - It never rates, criticizes or disparages the product. - It never implies partnership, sponsorship or endorsement. - A product’s name is used only to identify where the idea was seen. In the catalog, the note is the optional provenance field of a tool’s entry, and it is shown on the tool’s page.

title: Corrections and opt-outs
subtitle: Clean room and credit
summary: The maker of a product can ask for a factual correction, or ask not to be named. Requests go to contact@clearedstack.com or to a public issue on GitHub. A factu...
content: Corrections and opt-outs Clean room and credit The maker of a product can ask for a factual correction, or ask not to be named. Requests go to contact@clearedstack.com or to a public issue on GitHub. A factual error about a product is corrected once it is confirmed. A citation to public law is never removed, because it is not the vendor’s to withdraw.

content: The same rule for the platform’s own services Clean room and credit The clean-room rule also applies to the services the pipeline is designed to run on. Self-hosted platforms are usually assembled from large existing projects. This design instead specifies four small services written from scratch, which borrow ideas from those projects and none of their code. | Idea borrowed from | Service | What it does | | --- | --- | --- | | Forgejo | Plainforge | Holds the repositories, signals each push and mirrors code to GitHub | | Harbor and similar registries | Lazarette | Stores built images inside the cluster and keeps the last five of each | | Forgejo Actions | Keelworks | Builds and tests on each push, without a Docker daemon | | Argo CD and CasaOS | Shipkeeper | Deploys what was built, and offers install, upgrade, pause and rollback | Writing them fresh keeps every repository under one license, MIT, and keeps each service small enough to read. Cluster architecture describes them.

title: Cluster architecture

summary: The one-node, two-namespace cluster the pipeline is designed to run on: its seven control-plane services, how code is built and deployed without Docker, and where the data lives.
content: Cluster architecture The one-node, two-namespace cluster the pipeline is designed to run on: its seven control-plane services, how code is built and deployed without Docker, and where the data lives. cluster J.2 design  The pipeline is designed to run on a single small Kubernetes node, with everything it needs inside the cluster: its own Git server, its own image registry, its own build runner and its own deployer. This page describes that design. To run your own copy of this website, you need a web server and nothing else. See Host as plain files or Host on Kubernetes. This page is about the cluster for the pipeline that chooses and builds tools. One node, two namespaces, seventeen pods The whole platform is sized to fit on one machine with 4 GiB of memory, running k3s with containerd . | Namespace | What ru

subtitle: Cluster architecture
summary: The whole platform is sized to fit on one machine with 4 GiB of memory, running k3s with containerd . | Namespace | What runs there | Memory requested | | --- |...
content: One node, two namespaces, seventeen pods Cluster architecture The whole platform is sized to fit on one machine with 4 GiB of memory, running k3s with containerd . | Namespace | What runs there | Memory requested | | --- | --- | --- | | clearedstack | The control plane: seven services | About 640 MiB | | cs-workers | The pipeline: ten workers, plus short-lived browser jobs when a page needs one | About 300 MiB | Under 1 GiB at rest leaves room for the operating system, the database’s storage and the occasional build. An earlier draft gave every worker its own namespace, eleven in all. Two keeps the network rules simple and the manifests few, which matters to one person maintaining the stack.

The only service that can be reached from outside | 128 MiB | | Muster | Hands out work to the workers, records results and receives edit proposals | 48 MiB | | Logbook | The one database, on a persistent volume. Logbook is the record itself; today it is kept in PostgreSQL | 256 MiB | | Plainforge | Holds every repository, signals each push and mirrors code to GitHub | 64 MiB | | Lazarette | Stores built images inside the cluster and keeps the last five of each | 64 MiB | | Keelworks | Starts a short-lived job to test and build on each push | 32 MiB | | Shipkeeper | Deploys what was built, watches its health and reports it | 48 MiB | Plainforge, Lazarette, Keelworks and Shipkeeper are written from scratch as small Go programs instead of being assembled from large existing projects. Clean room and credit explains why.

title: From a push to a running pod
subtitle: Cluster architecture
summary: Every change follows the same path, and no step uses Docker. Why no Docker. A Docker daemon runs with root-level privileges and uses memory a small node cannot ...
content: From a push to a running pod Cluster architecture Every change follows the same path, and no step uses Docker. Why no Docker. A Docker daemon runs with root-level privileges and uses memory a small node cannot spare. Building images inside a cluster with Docker usually means giving the build job control of the host. k3s already runs containers with containerd , so all the cluster needs is a standard image, and there are builders that produce one without a daemon: | Builder | Used for | How | | --- | --- | --- | | ko | Everything written in Go: Plainforge, Lazarette, Keelworks, Shipkeeper, Muster and the ten workers | Compiles the source straight into a minimal image, with no build file and no daemon | | Rootless BuildKit | The website | Builds the image from the repository’s Containerfile inside an unprivileged pod | Tests come first. A build job runs the repository’s tests, including the saved examples for every sub-tool, before it builds anything. Code that fails never reaches the registry. Images are signed. Each image’s digest is signed with cosign before it is stored.

title: Code on GitHub, images inside
subtitle: Cluster architecture
summary: Plainforge is the primary copy of every repository. It sits inside the cluster and cannot be reached from the internet. Everything that writes code talks to it ...
content: Code on GitHub, images inside Cluster architecture Plainforge is the primary copy of every repository. It sits inside the cluster and cannot be reached from the internet. Everything that writes code talks to it first: an approved edit, a task for a missing rule, a new image digest. On each change it pushes the code outward to GitHub, so that anyone can read, check or fork it. GitHub is a mirror of the code only. Built images never leave the cluster. | | GitHub | Lazarette | | --- | --- | --- | | What is there | Source code and tags | Signed images | | How it gets there | Pushed outward by Plainforge on each change | Pushed by a build job, inside the cluster | | Rolling back | Would need a rebuild | Immediate, from the last five images kept | Keeping images inside means no registry passwords in the worker pods, and a rollback that works even when the outside network does not.

title: Install, upgrade, pause, roll back
subtitle: Cluster architecture
summary: Shipkeeper reads each app’s manifest from Plainforge and applies it to the cluster with Kubernetes’ own server-side apply. It adds no custom resource types. For...
content: Install, upgrade, pause, roll back Cluster architecture Shipkeeper reads each app’s manifest from Plainforge and applies it to the cluster with Kubernetes’ own server-side apply. It adds no custom resource types. For the owner it offers four actions on any service or worker: - Install applies the app’s manifests for the first time. - Upgrade moves it to the newest signed image. - Pause scales it down without deleting its configuration or data. - Rollback returns it to one of the five previous images kept in Lazarette. It also watches the health of every pod and reports it, after removing anything that would reveal the layout of the cluster. See what stays private.

title: One database and one gatekeeper
subtitle: Cluster architecture
summary: All state lives in a single Postgres database: the items, the queue, the decisions and the edit proposals. Keeping the queue and the state in one place means a ...
content: One database and one gatekeeper Cluster architecture All state lives in a single Postgres database: the items, the queue, the decisions and the edit proposals. Keeping the queue and the state in one place means a change of state and the next step in the queue happen together or not at all. An item is never marked done in one system while still waiting in another. The data is split in two. core holds the full working records. pub holds views of them with only the columns meant to be public. | Service | Access | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | Muster | Reads and writes core | It is the only gatekeeper in front of the database | | Conn | Reads pub only | The public site cannot reach a private field, whatever page is requested | | The ten workers | None | They hold no database password and cannot reach the database on the network | Workers ask Muster for work over the cluster’s private network and identify themselves with their Kubernetes service account. A worker that reads untrusted public pages therefore has no database credentials to leak. Only Muster knows the layout of the tables, so a change to a table does not ripple through ten repositories. Nothing finished is lost. Each worker has a small disk of its own. When it finishes a step it writes the result there first, then reports it. If Muster is restarting, the result waits on the worker’s disk and is sent again until it is acknowledged. Unfinished work is covered the other way round: the worker’s lease on the item runs out and the item is offered again.

title: Network, priority and privilege
subtitle: Cluster architecture
summary: Closed unless opened. Both namespaces block all traffic by default. Only Conn accepts connections from outside. Workers may call Muster, and the workers that re...
content: Network, priority and privilege Cluster architecture Closed unless opened. Both namespaces block all traffic by default. Only Conn accepts connections from outside. Workers may call Muster, and the workers that read public sources may fetch them from outside. Workers cannot reach the database, Plainforge or Lazarette. Who keeps running under pressure. | Priority | Workloads | When memory is short | | --- | --- | --- | | High | The database, the queue service, the website, Plainforge, Lazarette, Shipkeeper | Kept running, so the site and the queue stay up | | Standard | The ten workers | Give way before the control plane does | | Low | Build jobs and browser jobs | Run when there is room, and are stopped first | No root. Every pod runs as an ordinary user, with all Linux capabilities dropped, no way to gain privileges and a read-only filesystem wherever nothing needs to be written.

title: Starting from nothing
subtitle: Cluster architecture
summary: The design calls for the cluster to set itself up from one manifest applied to a fresh k3s node. A setup job that runs once then: | Step | What it does | Why | ...
content: Starting from nothing Cluster architecture The design calls for the cluster to set itself up from one manifest applied to a fresh k3s node. A setup job that runs once then: | Step | What it does | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | Secrets | Generates the database passwords, service tokens, signing keys and the salt used to hash visitor addresses | Credentials are created inside the cluster and never appear in Git | | Database | Creates the core tables and the pub views | Private data and public data are separate from the first minute | | Repositories | Creates a repository in Plainforge for each service and worker | The cluster has its own source of truth | | First builds | Has Keelworks build and sign every image | Nothing is pulled ready-made from outside | | Network rules | Applies the rules that leave only the website reachable | The database, Git, the registry and the workers are closed from the start | Because every repository is MIT licensed and written from scratch, the design can be forked without asking: rebranded, given different scoring weights, or run privately with the GitHub mirror turned off.

title: Running it with no internet connection
subtitle: Cluster architecture
summary: Nothing in the design depends on an outside service while it runs, so the whole cluster can sit inside a closed network. Four things change. | Part | Connected ...
content: Running it with no internet connection Cluster architecture Nothing in the design depends on an outside service while it runs, so the whole cluster can sit inside a closed network. Four things change. | Part | Connected | Disconnected | | --- | --- | --- | | Plainforge | Mirrors code to GitHub | The mirror is off. All code stays inside | | Tidegauge | Checks public regulation feeds | Paused, or pointed at copies kept inside | | Sextant | Fetches public pages | Reads only what can be reached inside, or files brought in | | Lazarette | Stores images built by Keelworks | The same. Nothing is pulled from outside | What crosses the boundary is a bundle of signed image archives, the manifests and the repositories, with a checksum to prove it arrived intact. Working on disconnected networks covers that discipline.

content: Conn specification Unified Command Portal, App Store UI, and anonymous edit intake serving as the sole public Ingress in the clearedstack namespace. components J.4 design formerly clearedstack-web  Shows the catalog, the guides and the state of the factory to anyone, and takes in edit proposals. Conn ( v0.2.0-draft , owned by clearedstack.com ) is the public-facing web application in the clearedstack control-plane namespace. It serves the contractor-first tool catalog, operational Command Portal, App Store UI, and anonymous ✎ Edit intake without requiring user accounts or logins. Overview & Role Conn is the only pod in the entire 17-pod cluster exposed to the public internet via the Kubernetes Ingress. Its responsibilities are strictly presentation, read-only public data rendering, and client-side intake framing: - Command Portal & Catalog: Serves the unified tool catalog ( /tools/ ),

title: Overview & Role
subtitle: Conn specification
summary: Conn is the only pod in the entire 17-pod cluster exposed to the public internet via the Kubernetes Ingress. Its responsibilities are strictly presentation, rea...
content: Overview & Role Conn specification Conn is the only pod in the entire 17-pod cluster exposed to the public internet via the Kubernetes Ingress. Its responsibilities are strictly presentation, read-only public data rendering, and client-side intake framing: - Command Portal & Catalog: Serves the unified tool catalog ( /tools/ ), operational guides ( /guides/ ), live P0–P2 attention feed, and App Store UI. - Zero Login Lock: All browsing, queue inspection, sanitized error viewing, and edit proposals work anonymously without accounts, passwords, or OAuth redirects. - Sanitized Read-Only Queries: Reads exclusively from sanitized pub. views in Logbook—never touching core. internal tables or cluster secrets. - Anonymous Edit Intake UI: Uses ownership map.json to map any editable element on the page to its owning repository ( clearedstack.com or Trawl through Bellbuoy) and change class ( DATA , CONFIG , or ISSUE ), then forwards proposals to Muster.

title: Interfaces & Data Contracts
subtitle: Conn specification
summary: Conn sits at the edge of the clearedstack namespace and communicates with two internal control-plane services: | Peer Service | Direction | Protocol / Role | Da...
content: Interfaces & Data Contracts Conn specification Conn sits at the edge of the clearedstack namespace and communicates with two internal control-plane services: | Peer Service | Direction | Protocol / Role | Data Contract | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Cluster Ingress | Inbound | HTTPS (Public) | Serves static/SSR Portal pages, /tools/ , /guides/ , and anonymous ✎ Edit forms | | Logbook | Outbound | SQL ( pub ro role) | Read-only SELECT access to sanitized pub. views only; zero access to core. | | Muster | Bidirectional | Cluster-private HTTP + SSE | Subscribes to Server-Sent Events (SSE) for live queue/status updates; submits ✎ Edit payloads (with ~1s browser Proof-of-Work token and honeypot field) | Live Edit Status Tracking After a visitor submits an anonymous edit, Conn turns the element's ✎ Edit button into a live status pill backed by Muster SSE events: 1. Proposed: Passed 5-layer anti-spam and ownership map.json schema checks; waiting in Countersign. 2. Approved: Approved by the owner and routed via Bellbuoy to Plainforge. 3. Building: Keelworks is running deterministic tests and packaging the updated image. 4. Live: Shipkeeper reconciled the new digest and the updated content is live.

title: Failure Modes & Recovery
subtitle: Conn specification
summary: - Pod Crash or OOMKill: Because Conn is stateless with no PVC, k3s restarts the pod automatically. High Priority Class protects it from preemption during Keelwo...
content: Failure Modes & Recovery Conn specification - Pod Crash or OOMKill: Because Conn is stateless with no PVC, k3s restarts the pod automatically. High Priority Class protects it from preemption during Keelworks builds or Sextant headless browser Jobs. - Muster Unavailable / SSE Drop: If Muster restarts during a rolling upgrade, the SSE stream drops and the UI surfaces a stale-feed indicator (P1 attention triggers if the live feed is stale for more than 15 seconds) while pub. views remain readable from Logbook. - Logbook Unavailable: Public pages that depend on pub. views degrade gracefully until Logbook recovers; no write state is lost because Conn never writes to the database.

title: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries
subtitle: Conn specification
summary: - Only Public Door: Default-deny NetworkPolicy blocks Ingress traffic to every other pod in clearedstack and cs-workers . - Database Isolation: Connects to Logb...
content: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries Conn specification - Only Public Door: Default-deny NetworkPolicy blocks Ingress traffic to every other pod in clearedstack and cs-workers . - Database Isolation: Connects to Logbook solely with the pub ro role, which has zero privileges on core. tables, credentials, or internal operational state. - No Topology Leakage: Never receives raw node names, pod hostnames, or internal cluster IPs; Shipkeeper strips those fields before status reaches Muster and pub. . - Unprivileged Execution: Runs as a non-root user with dropped Linux capabilities, no privilege escalation, and a read-only root filesystem where state does not need to be written. - Anti-Spam Framing: Enforces client-side Proof-of-Work (~1s cryptographic puzzle) and a hidden honeypot field before forwarding anonymous edit proposals to Muster.

content: Countersign specification Technical specification for Countersign, the human-accountability queue worker powering tool determinations and anonymous edit approvals on /guides/#decide. components J.4 design formerly cs-04-decide Gavel Holds scored candidates and edit proposals until a person decides. Implemented in the Countersign repository under the MIT License, it records authoritative human determinations for evaluated candidates and gates visitor-submitted ✎ edit proposals before any code or configuration touches Plainforge. Unlike upstream automated workers, Countersign never makes autonomous judgment calls: final accountability for building, linking, merging, parking

content: Overview & Role Countersign specification Countersign ( v0.1.0-draft ) powers the human owner's decision and anonymous edit-approval inbox surfaced on /platform/public-edits/ and /platform/public-edits/ , replacing the original Stage 6 (Decide). content: Interfaces & State Transitions Countersign specification Countersign interacts with Muster in the clearedstack namespace over ServiceAccount-authenticated HTTP ( CONTRACT VERSION=v1 ) and surfaces two transparent queues via pub. read-only views on clearedstack.com : 1. Tool Determinations Queue ( scored and screened-out overrides): - Approve (Build) → approved : Advances the candidate to Waybill for provenance stamping and clean-room spec compilation. - Link → linked : Records an existing free, private external tool in the catalog (Chartroom) without rebuilding. - Merge → merged : Folds scope into an existing or planned parent tool repository. - Park → parked : Defers a viable idea with a named blocker for scheduled Tidegauge revisit. - Reject → rejected : Permanently archives the candidate with its rubric score and rationale. - Override → observed : Returns a screened-out item to observed only when accompanied by an explicit written reason logged publicly. 2. Anonymous Public Edit Proposals ( core.edit proposal , pending approval ): - Receives DATA , CONFIG , and ISSUE proposals (≤ 4 KB) submitted via any ✎ button after they clear Muster's 5-layer anti-spam shield. - On owner Approve , dispatches Bellbuoy on the urgent lane ( Proposed → Approved → Building → Live ). Declined proposals are logged without altering Plainforge or core. data.

Sanitized Failure Modes | Error Code | Trigger | Platform Behavior | | --- | --- | --- | | E PARSE | Malformed determination payload, missing written rationale on an override, or invalid ownership map.json target on an edit proposal. | Rejected cleanly by Muster; item remains in its current queue state with a fingerprinted error logged. | | E TIMEOUT | Transient timeout reaching Muster during decision commit. | Buffered in /var/spool/cs and retried in order until acknowledged. | Because Countersign has no tools// sub-tools, it never enters needs subtool ( E NEEDS SUBTOOL ).

title: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries
subtitle: Countersign specification

content: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries Countersign specification - 5-layer anti-spam gate before Countersign: Anonymous ✎ edit proposals must pass browser Proof-of-Work, a hidden honeypot field, daily-salted IP hash rate limiting (zero raw IPs stored), and strict 4 KB schema validation against ownership map.json (with HTML/scripts stripped) before entering pending approval . - Zero unreviewed cluster mutations: No anonymous edit or external submission can touch Plainforge, core. state, or running pods until explicitly approved in Countersign. - Public accountability & pod hardening: All decisions, overrides, and edit outcomes are visible in read-only pub. views without login. The pod runs non-root with dropped capabilities, a read-only root filesystem (except /var/spool/cs ), zero database credentials, and default-deny NetworkPolicy .

title: The five choices that shaped the design
subtitle: What is decided and what is open
summary: The design was reviewed from five points of view before it was settled: running a Kubernetes platform, designing a live interface, queue systems, security and c...
content: The five choices that shaped the design What is decided and what is open The design was reviewed from five points of view before it was settled: running a Kubernetes platform, designing a live interface, queue systems, security and compliance, and what one maintainer can realistically keep going. Each main choice came out of a trade-off between them. | Question | First assumption | What was decided | Why | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | A description or a system | Essays describing ten stages | Ten workers, one for each stage, whose state can be shown | A reader should be able to see what the process is doing, not only read about it | | Where state lives | A database for each stage | One shared database, one service in front of it, and a small disk on each worker | Workers hold no database password, a hand-off cannot half-happen, and finished work survives a restart | | Git, builds and deployment | Large existing projects | Four small services written from scratch | The control plane fits in about 640 MiB, so the whole platform fits on one 4 GiB machine | | Awkward cases | AI inside the workers | Fixed rules everywhere, and stop when no rule applies | No running cost for a model, the same result on every machine, and each solved case becomes permanent code | | Public access | A login to propose edits | No login, five automatic checks and a person’s approval | Anyone can inspect and improve the work, while addresses and credentials stay hidden | Why not assemble it from existing projects. A Git forge, a registry, a deployment controller and an app dashboard taken off the shelf would have needed several times the memory before the pipeline did any work, and would have brought a mix of licenses. Four single-purpose services keep the control plane small, remove Docker altogether and keep every repository under MIT. See Clean room and credit. Why two namespaces and not eleven. An early draft gave the hub and each worker a namespace of its own. Two namespaces give the same separation between the control plane and the workers with far fewer manifests to maintain.

content: How we decide what to build The five knockout gates an idea has to pass, the 100-point rubric it is scored on, how ties are broken, and who makes the final decision. factory J.1 design  Section M of a solicitation tells bidders how their proposals will be judged. This page is the same thing for ideas: the complete set of rules by which a candidate tool is screened, scored and decided. The rules are public so that anyone can see why one tool was built and another was not. The screening and scoring are done by fixed rules with no AI, so the same facts always give the same score. The decision is made by a person. The five knockout gates Before any points are counted, a candidate has to pass five yes-or-no tests. Failing one ends the evaluation, and the reason is recorded. 1. Pub

title: The five knockout gates
subtitle: How we decide what to build
summary: Before any points are counted, a candidate has to pass five yes-or-no tests. Failing one ends the evaluation, and the reason is recorded. 1. Public source. Its ...
content: The five knockout gates How we decide what to build Before any points are counted, a candidate has to pass five yes-or-no tests. Failing one ends the evaluation, and the reason is recorded. 1. Public source. Its rules, formulas and thresholds come from officially released material: statutes, the FAR, the DFARS, NIST publications. Not a paywalled manual, and not industry folklore. 2. Runs in the browser. It can work entirely on the user’s machine, with no server and no outside service. 3. Private by design. It works offline, needs no account, tracks nothing and can enforce a content security policy that blocks outside requests. 4. One job. It does a single task that can be described in one sentence starting with a verb. A suite fails, unless it is split into smaller ideas. 5. Arithmetic, not advice. It computes, structures or looks things up. It does not give legal advice or stand in for a contracting officer’s judgment.

Each rating is multiplied by the factor’s weight, giving a total between 20 and 100. | Factor | Weight | A rating of 1 | A rating of 3 | A rating of 5 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Need for small businesses | ×4, up to 20 | A rare edge case | Comes up now and then, such as once a year | A recurring obstacle for most small contractors, costly when done wrong | | Gap: no free, private option exists | ×4, up to 20 | Good free tools that run on the user’s machine already exist | A clumsy government portal, or open tools that are hard to use | Only paid products or lead-capture forms exist | | Strength of the public source | ×3, up to 15 | An informal slide deck or an unclear draft | A policy memo or an interim rule | A statute, a codified regulation or a published standard | | Fits in a browser | ×3, up to 15 | Needs very large data or heavy computing | Needs moderate bundled tables or a special parser | Simple arithmetic or text handling with very little data | | Small enough to read | ×2, up to 10 | A sprawling program with many settings | Moderate, with clear inputs and outputs | Short enough to read in one sitting | | Can be checked | ×2, up to 10 | Rests on interpretation | A formula with edge cases that need warnings | Plain arithmetic with official worked examples to test against | | Low upkeep | ×2, up to 10 | Needs frequent data updates or fragile page reading | Updated once a year | Rests on text that changes only when the rule is amended |

title: The decision is a person’s
subtitle: How we decide what to build
summary: The score is a recommendation. The owner reviews each scored candidate and chooses one of the outcomes: build, link, merge into another tool, park or reject. Th...
content: The decision is a person’s How we decide what to build The score is a recommendation. The owner reviews each scored candidate and chooses one of the outcomes: build, link, merge into another tool, park or reject. The owner can also override the recommendation, or reopen a candidate that was screened out. An override needs a written reason, and the reason is recorded in the public decision log.

content: Where the rules come from How we decide what to build Each area of the catalog has its own profile of thresholds for the rubric: pricing, proposals, cyber, market research and DevSecOps. A candidate in an area with no profile is not scored by guesswork. It is paused until a profile is written, the same way any worker handles a case it has no rule for. See The pipeline and its ten workers. To suggest a tool, see Request a tool or add your own. How often a tool is asked for is the fifth tie-breaker above.

title: What does not get lost
subtitle: An item’s life: fourteen states and three lanes
summary: Two things protect work in progress. An item a worker has claimed goes back in the queue if that worker stops, because its lease runs out. And a result a worker...
content: What does not get lost An item’s life: fourteen states and three lanes Two things protect work in progress. An item a worker has claimed goes back in the queue if that worker stops, because its lease runs out. And a result a worker has finished is kept on the worker’s own disk until the queue service confirms it has it, so a restart in the middle loses nothing. Cluster architecture describes both.

subtitle: Keelworks specification
summary: Keelworks coordinates four internal control-plane interfaces: 1. Webhook Intake (Plainforge -> Keelworks): Receives cluster-private push and tag webhooks from P...
content: Interfaces & Data Contracts Keelworks specification Keelworks coordinates four internal control-plane interfaces: 1. Webhook Intake (Plainforge -> Keelworks): Receives cluster-private push and tag webhooks from Plainforge. Commits containing [skip-ci] in the commit message are ignored to prevent recursive build loops. 2. Ephemeral Job Orchestration (Kubernetes API): Spawns short-lived Job pods in clearedstack with the appropriate builder: - ko : Compiles Go binaries (Plainforge, Lazarette, Keelworks, Shipkeeper, Muster, and Trawl through Bellbuoy) directly into minimal OCI images with zero Dockerfile or Docker daemon. - Rootless BuildKit: Builds multi-layer container images for Next.js web workloads (Conn) inside an unprivileged, rootless pod. 3. Test, Sign & Push ( Job -> Lazarette): Executes golden fixture tests before building. Passing builds are signed with cosign and pushed by sha256 digest to Lazarette. 4. Manifest Pinning (Keelworks -> Plainforge): Updates the pinned image digest in app.yaml inside Plainforge with a [skip-ci] commit so Shipkeeper can reconcile the new release.

content: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries Keelworks specification - Zero Docker daemon: No Docker socket ( /var/run/docker.sock ), privileged containers, or root-level build daemons exist anywhere on the host or inside build Job pods. - Rootless & unprivileged: Both the Keelworks controller and its spawned ko / rootless BuildKit Job s run as non-root users with dropped Linux capabilities and no privilege escalation. - Cluster-private only: Keelworks has no public Ingress and accepts webhooks exclusively from Plainforge under default-deny NetworkPolicy rules. - Supply-chain integrity: Every published image is tested against golden fixtures and cryptographically signed with cosign before app.yaml is updated.

content: Interfaces & Data Contracts Lazarette specification Lazarette exposes a cluster-private HTTP interface ( ClusterIP only, no public Ingress) implementing standard OCI Distribution Specification ( /v2/ ) endpoints: - Image Push (Keelworks build jobs): Accepts OCI image manifests, config blobs, and layers from ephemeral ko and rootless BuildKit Job pods, along with cosign signature artifacts. - Image Pull ( containerd / k3s ): Serves signed image manifests and layers by immutable sha256 digest when Shipkeeper deploys or rolls back workloads. - Retention & Digest Index (Shipkeeper): Retains the last 5 signed digests per app so Shipkeeper can execute 1-click rollbacks from /platform/ registry without triggering a rebuild. - Daily Garbage Collection: Runs a scheduled cleanup pass to remove unreferenced layers and manifests older than the 5 retained digests per app, keeping PVC disk usage predictable on a single-node cluster.

content: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries Lazarette specification - Cluster-private network boundary: Lazarette has no public Ingress. Default-deny Kubernetes NetworkPolicy rules restrict access to internal cluster traffic only (Keelworks pushing, Shipkeeper inspecting digests, and containerd pulling). - Zero external image leakage: Source code is mirrored to GitHub via Plainforge, but built OCI binaries and layers remain strictly inside the clearedstack namespace. - Unprivileged execution: Runs as a non-root user with dropped Linux capabilities, no privilege escalation, and a read-only root filesystem (writable only on the mounted OCI storage PVC). - Immutable digest addressing: Workloads are pinned in app.yaml by sha256 digest rather than mutable :latest tags.

title: Logbook specification
subtitle: Platform · Section J.4
summary: The platform’s one record of state: the working records, the public views of them and the append-only ledger, kept today in a single PostgreSQL 17 database.
content: Logbook specification The platform’s one record of state: the working records, the public views of them and the append-only ledger, kept today in a single PostgreSQL 17 database. components J.4 design formerly postgres  Keeps the record of every item, decision and proposal, and the public views of that record. Logbook is the name for the platform’s record of state, not for the database engine. If PostgreSQL were ever replaced, Logbook would still be Logbook. Today it is a single shared PostgreSQL 17 database (image postgres:17-alpine , with its schema owned by clearedstack.com ). Running one consolidated database on a Persistent Volume Claim (PVC) eliminates multi-database sync bugs and keeps control-plane memory compact enough for a single 4 GiB k3s node. Overview & Role Logbook is the durable system of record for live operational state, work queues, and sanitized public views: - Single Source of T

title: Failure Modes & Recovery
subtitle: Logbook specification
summary: Because Logbook holds one of the cluster's three non-recreatable Persistent Volume Claims, durability and recovery are verified continuously rather than assumed...
content: Failure Modes & Recovery Logbook specification Because Logbook holds one of the cluster's three non-recreatable Persistent Volume Claims, durability and recovery are verified continuously rather than assumed: - Consistent Nightly Backups: A scheduled backup job takes a consistent database dump (never a raw file copy while writes are active), encrypts the dump client-side with age , transfers it to off-node storage, and prunes old snapshots on a fixed retention schedule. - Automated Monthly Restore Drill: Once a month, the cluster provisions an isolated scratch area, downloads the latest age -encrypted backup, decrypts it with the current key, restores Logbook from scratch, and runs deterministic integrity checks on core. tables and pub. views before tearing down the scratch environment. - Live Drill Visibility: The timestamp and pass/fail outcome of the four monthly verification checks are published directly to the live Portal so backup drift surfaces immediately. - Pod Restart / Node Reboot: Because data resides on the PVC and Logbook runs under the High Priority Class, k3s reattaches the volume and recovers cleanly via PostgreSQL crash recovery.

title: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries
subtitle: Logbook specification
summary: - Default-Deny Network Isolation: NetworkPolicy blocks all pods in cs-workers and all external Ingress traffic from reaching Logbook on the network. - Least-Pri...
content: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries Logbook specification - Default-Deny Network Isolation: NetworkPolicy blocks all pods in cs-workers and all external Ingress traffic from reaching Logbook on the network. - Least-Privilege Roles: Conn is restricted to pub ro on pub. views, ensuring no public query can ever read core. tables, internal tokens, or unapproved edit payloads. - Encrypted Off-Node Backups: Backup archives are encrypted with age before leaving the host node, with the decryption key stored separately from the off-node backup target. - Unprivileged Execution: Runs as non-root with dropped capabilities and no privilege escalation.

Generates the isolated static tool repository (including LICENSE under MIT, bundled lookup tables, strict CSP headers default-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; form-action 'none' , regulatory citations, scope limits, and worked-example tests) and routes it to Plainforge (mirrored to GitHub on change, with zero container images pushed to GitHub). 4. title: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries
subtitle: Moldloft specification
summary: - Absolute clean-room isolation: Muster enforces the shared contract boundary by rejecting any payload containing raw Sextant HTML, screenshots, or snapshots be...
content: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries Moldloft specification - Absolute clean-room isolation: Muster enforces the shared contract boundary by rejecting any payload containing raw Sextant HTML, screenshots, or snapshots before Moldloft can lease it. Moldloft never accesses vendor sites or observation archives. - Synthetic fixtures only: Worked-example test fixtures must use hand-calculated official examples, boundary cases, and synthetic data. Real CUI, proprietary contractor rates, and non-public solicitation text are strictly forbidden. - Generated tool security: Every generated static tool enforces connect-src 'self' , default-src 'self' , form-action 'none' , zero tracking/analytics, and offline execution. - Pod hardening & network policy: Runs non-root with dropped capabilities, read-only root filesystem (except /var/spool/cs ), zero database credentials, and default-deny NetworkPolicy permitting only ServiceAccount HTTP to Muster (no direct access to Logbook, Plainforge, or Lazarette).

content: Muster specification Central queue lease manager, state-transition gatekeeper, SSE live feed publisher, and 5-layer anti-spam edit intake in the clearedstack namespace. components J.4 design formerly hub-queue-api  Hands out work to the workers, records every result and change of state, and receives edit proposals. summary: - Hub Restart During Worker Execution: Because Muster is a single control-plane pod, a rolling upgrade or restart makes it briefly unreachable. Workers stage co...
content: Failure Modes & Recovery Muster specification - Hub Restart During Worker Execution: Because Muster is a single control-plane pod, a rolling upgrade or restart makes it briefly unreachable. Workers stage completed outputs in their local spool volume first, then retry delivery to Muster on a short backoff until acknowledged, deleting the spooled file only after Postgres confirms receipt. - Worker Crash Mid-Lease: If a worker pod dies before acknowledging a task, its lease expires in Logbook and Muster re-leases the unfinished item to a healthy worker. - SSE Disconnect or Stale Feed: If the SSE stream to Conn stalls for more than 15 seconds, deterministic attention rules surface a P1 warning on the Command Portal. - High-Load Contention: High Priority Class keeps Muster scheduled ahead of workers and ephemeral Jobs when node memory tightens.
