content: Operating it: status views, failures and backups The fixed rules that decide what a status page shows first, what happens when a worker fails, and how the three stores of data are backed up and tested. cluster J.2 design  A platform that one person runs has to say plainly when something is wrong, stay quiet when nothing is, and recover without heroics. This page covers the three parts of the design that deal with that: the rules for the status views, the path a failure takes, and backups. What a status view shows first A dashboard is useless if healthy background noise hides a real failure. In this design, what appears at the top of a status page is decided by five fixed rules, not by a person arranging charts and not by a model guessing what looks important. The same state of the cluster always produces the sa

title: What a status view shows first
subtitle: Operating it: status views, failures and backups
summary: A dashboard is useless if healthy background noise hides a real failure. In this design, what appears at the top of a status page is decided by five fixed rules...
content: What a status view shows first Operating it: status views, failures and backups A dashboard is useless if healthy background noise hides a real failure. In this design, what appears at the top of a status page is decided by five fixed rules, not by a person arranging charts and not by a model guessing what looks important. The same state of the cluster always produces the same page. | Priority | Name | What triggers it | How it is shown | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | P0 | Critical | A pod crashes, a health check fails, or an item cannot be processed at all | At the top, in red, with the error code and a rollback control for the owner | | P1 | Stalled | A worker is paused waiting for a rule, a queue is backed up, or the feed of updates has been silent for more than 15 seconds | Beside P0, in amber, with the error code and the repository that owns the fix | | P2 | Needs a person | Candidates are waiting for a decision, or proposals are waiting for approval | Listed with how long the oldest has waited | | P3 | Working | Workers are processing items with no errors | In green, with counts | | P4 | Quiet | A healthy worker has nothing to do | Folded into one muted line |

title: Six states, never disguised
subtitle: Operating it: status views, failures and backups
summary: Every component on a status page is in exactly one of six states. An idle worker is never painted red, and missing data is never shown as healthy. | State | Loo...
content: Six states, never disguised Operating it: status views, failures and backups Every component on a status page is in exactly one of six states. An idle worker is never painted red, and missing data is never shown as healthy. | State | Looks like | Means | | --- | --- | --- | | healthy | Green | Running, passing its checks, and reporting on time | | idle | Muted grey | Healthy and ready, with nothing to do | | erroring | Red, with a code | An active failure. Shows a code such as E TIMEOUT , never a stack trace or an address | | recovering | Amber | Retrying after an error, or waiting for a missing rule | | stale | Dashed outline | No update for more than 15 seconds. The view is paused, not live | | empty | Muted placeholder | Nothing has been collected yet | Numbers that do not flicker. Three guards keep a live page readable. A status has to hold for about two minutes before its color changes, so one brief spike does not flip a label back and forth. Updates are sent in small batches every few seconds instead of one at a time. And every figure carries the time it was produced, so a number that has stopped updating is shown as stale instead of sitting there looking current.

title: When a worker fails
subtitle: Operating it: status views, failures and backups
summary: Because no worker guesses, a failure is a predictable sequence instead of a mystery. The three error codes. | Code | In plain terms | What happens next | | --- ...
content: When a worker fails Operating it: status views, failures and backups Because no worker guesses, a failure is a predictable sequence instead of a mystery. The three error codes. | Code | In plain terms | What happens next | | --- | --- | --- | | E TIMEOUT | Something took too long: an outside site, a download, an internal step | The item stays in the queue and can be tried again without losing earlier progress | | E PARSE | The data was broken: malformed, or a damaged file | The worker refuses to guess, records the failure and stops work on that item | | E NEEDS SUBTOOL | The data was fine but unfamiliar, such as a table laid out in a new way | The item is paused until a rule is written, then run again. See Sub-tools | Two switches for the owner. | Action | What it does | When to use it | | --- | --- | --- | | Pause | Stops the worker without deleting its queue or its settings | An outside site is down, or you want retries to stop while you look | | Rollback | Returns the worker to one of the last five images kept inside the cluster | A new version made things worse and you want the last good one back | A rollback needs nothing from outside the cluster, so it works when the outside network does not.

title: Backups
subtitle: Operating it: status views, failures and backups
summary: Most of the platform holds no data of its own. If the website, the build runner or a worker stops, a fresh copy is started and nothing is lost. Everything that ...
content: Backups Operating it: status views, failures and backups Most of the platform holds no data of its own. If the website, the build runner or a worker stops, a fresh copy is started and nothing is lost. Everything that cannot be recreated lives in three places. | Store | Holds | Why it cannot simply be rebuilt | | --- | --- | --- | | The database | The queue, each item’s history, the scores, the decisions and the proposals | It is the record of everything that has been decided | | Plainforge | Every repository, including each app’s manifest | It is the primary copy. GitHub has the code, not necessarily the latest commit | | Lazarette | The signed images | Images are not on GitHub. Without them nothing can roll back until everything is rebuilt | Every night , a job takes a consistent copy of all three and sends it off the machine. | Stage | What happens | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | Consistent copy | The database is dumped at a single moment, and the two volumes are archived | A database copied while it is being written to can be unusable | | Encrypted before it leaves | The archives are encrypted on the machine | A leaked backup is unreadable without the key, which is kept somewhere else | | Sent elsewhere | The encrypted bundles go to storage off the machine | Losing the machine does not lose the backups too | | Old copies removed | Older backups are dropped on a fixed schedule | Storage stays predictable |

title: A restore drill every month
subtitle: Operating it: status views, failures and backups
summary: A backup that has never been restored is a hope. Backups fail quietly: a key is changed and no longer matches, a table changes shape and breaks an old script, a...
content: A restore drill every month Operating it: status views, failures and backups A backup that has never been restored is a hope. Backups fail quietly: a key is changed and no longer matches, a table changes shape and breaks an old script, a disk fills halfway through an archive. The usual time to find out is the worst one. So once a month the design restores everything for real, into a temporary space separate from the running system. It fetches the latest backups, decrypts them, restores all three stores from scratch, checks them and then removes the temporary space. | Check | What it verifies | What a pass proves | | --- | --- | --- | | Decrypt and unpack | The archive downloads and opens with the current key | The backup is readable and the key has not drifted | | Database | It loads without errors and its tables pass integrity checks | The queue, the items and the decisions are intact | | Plainforge | The repositories pass Git’s own consistency check | The code and the manifests are whole | | Lazarette | The image manifests and signatures resolve | Components can start and roll back without the internet | The result of each drill is meant to be published: when it ran, whether it passed, and the outcome of each of the four checks. A broken backup should show up as a visible warning, not as a surprise during an outage.

content: How the project is put together The parts of the factory behind the catalog, the path from an idea to a listed tool, and the four rules everything else follows. factory J.1 design  The catalog is the part of ClearedStack a contractor sees. Behind it is a design for choosing and building tools in the open: a pipeline of ten small programs that finds ideas, screens and scores them, and builds each tool from the public rule, on a small cluster that anyone can copy. This page is the map. The other pages in this section fill in each part. The parts The project is split into small repositories, each with one job. | Group | Repositories | What it holds | | --- | --- | --- | | The hub | clearedstack.com | This website, the catalog, the guides, and the shared rules the other part

title: The parts
subtitle: How the project is put together
summary: The project is split into small repositories, each with one job. | Group | Repositories | What it holds | | --- | --- | --- | | The hub | clearedstack.com | Thi...
content: The parts How the project is put together The project is split into small repositories, each with one job. | Group | Repositories | What it holds | | --- | --- | --- | | The hub | clearedstack.com | This website, the catalog, the guides, and the shared rules the other parts agree on | | The pipeline | Trawl, Sextant, Assay, Countersign, Waybill, Moldloft, Shakedown, Chartroom, Tidegauge, Bellbuoy | Ten workers, one for each stage from finding an idea to watching a published tool | | The control plane | Plainforge, Lazarette, Keelworks, Shipkeeper | Four small services that hold the code, build it, store the images and deploy them | | The tools | One repository for each tool | The browser tools themselves, each able to be read, forked and hosted alone | Keeping the parts separate has three effects. A change to one worker rebuilds and redeploys only that worker. The worker that looks at existing tools and the worker that builds new ones live in different repositories, which is how the clean-room rule is enforced. And any one part can be rolled back without touching the rest. Every component has a name of its own, so that it can be understood and used without the rest. The naming registry lists all seventeen with what each is responsible for, what it depends on and what it used to be called.

title: Three loops that keep it current
subtitle: How the project is put together
summary: A catalog decays. Regulations change, the pages a worker reads are redesigned, and readers spot mistakes. The design turns each of those into a loop that ends i...
content: Three loops that keep it current How the project is put together A catalog decays. Regulations change, the pages a worker reads are redesigned, and readers spot mistakes. The design turns each of those into a loop that ends in a tested change. - A page no rule covers. A worker never guesses. It pauses the item, and a task is opened to write a rule for that case. When the rule ships, the paused items run again. See Sub-tools. - An edit from a reader. Anyone can propose a change without an account. Nothing is applied until the owner approves it. See Public edits. - A change in the rules. A watcher compares official sources on a schedule. When a cited clause changes, the affected tool is sent back to be checked and rebuilt. See Tidegauge.

title: Four rules everything follows
subtitle: How the project is put together
summary: 1. No AI when it runs. No worker and no tool calls an AI model. The same input gives the same output on any machine, and every result can be traced to a line of...
content: Four rules everything follows How the project is put together 1. No AI when it runs. No worker and no tool calls an AI model. The same input gives the same output on any machine, and every result can be traced to a line of code. AI is used only to help write that code, under review. See How AI is used. 2. Stop instead of guessing. A worker that meets something it has no rule for pauses that item and says why. In contracting, a guess is worse than a gap. 3. Hide the network, show the logic. The code, the rules, the scores and the decisions are public. Addresses, credentials and the layout of the cluster are not. See what stays private. 4. One person is accountable. The pipeline recommends. A named human owner decides, and overrides are written down with a reason.

content: The pipeline and its ten workers What each of the ten workers does, why none of them uses AI, how a case no rule covers is handled, and how the workers stay in step. factory J.1 design  The pipeline is ten small Go programs, from Trawl at stage 01 to Bellbuoy at stage 10, each in its own MIT-licensed repository and each with one job. Together they take an idea for a tool from first sighting to a listing in the catalog, and keep watching it afterward. This page describes each worker and the rules they share. Each name in the table links to that worker’s full specification, and the naming registry lists what each one used to be called. title: Finding and recording
subtitle: The pipeline and its ten workers
summary: Trawl collects candidates from four places: public notices on SAM.gov, issues opened on GitHub, scheduled sweeps of public government and vendor sites, and the ...
content: Finding and recording The pipeline and its ten workers Trawl collects candidates from four places: public notices on SAM.gov, issues opened on GitHub, scheduled sweeps of public government and vendor sites, and the form on this site. Its job is to make sure each one is recorded exactly once. Cleaning the address. The same tool is often reachable at several addresses. Before anything is saved, the address is put through fixed rules: the scheme and host are made lowercase, tracking and session parameters are removed along with any fragment, and trailing slashes and default file names are tidied so that equivalent addresses become one. Addresses that are not public, that point inside a private network or that need a login are refused. Checking for a duplicate. A SHA-256 hash of the cleaned address is compared with the ones already recorded. If it matches, the sighting is noted against the existing record. If it is new, the candidate is given a permanent identifier of the form PA-0001 and passed on. What intake never does. It does not create accounts on other sites, ask for sales demonstrations, get around a paywall or a CAPTCHA, ignore robots.txt , or accept controlled information or real bid figures.

title: Observing
subtitle: The pipeline and its ten workers
summary: Sextant reads what a candidate says about itself in public and turns that into a structured record: the job it does, its inputs and outputs, whether it needs a ...
content: Observing The pipeline and its ten workers Sextant reads what a candidate says about itself in public and turns that into a structured record: the job it does, its inputs and outputs, whether it needs a login, whether it tracks its users, its license, its price model, the public rule it cites and the date it was looked at. A small program first, a browser only when needed. Most public pages and documents can be read with a plain web request, by a program that needs about 30 MiB of memory. Only when a page is built entirely by scripts does the worker start a temporary browser to render it, and that browser is discarded as soon as the page has been read. Public pages only. The worker reads what anyone can see. It does not sign up, start a trial, fill in a contact form, enter real data or get past a login. Where a page says something the worker cannot see for itself, the fact is recorded as Stated instead of Seen . Anything else is Unknown . The raw page stays behind. The worker keeps the page it fetched only long enough to extract the facts. The copy is sealed and no later worker can read it. Only the structured record moves on. Clean room and credit explains why this matters.

content: Crediting and specifying The pipeline and its ten workers Once the owner approves a build, Waybill writes two things: the note that credits where the idea came from, and the specification the tool will be built from. The specification contains the official rule, the inputs and outputs, and worked examples. It contains nothing from the product that was observed. See Clean room and credit.

title: Building, verifying and listing
subtitle: The pipeline and its ten workers
summary: Building. Moldloft reads the specification and generates the tool’s own repository from one of four templates. | Template | Used for | In and out | | --- | --- ...
content: Building, verifying and listing The pipeline and its ten workers Building. Moldloft reads the specification and generates the tool’s own repository from one of four templates. | Template | Used for | In and out | | --- | --- | --- | | calculator | Rate build-ups, interest, thresholds | Numbers or dates in; the working and a cited total out | | checklist | Solicitation reviews, compliance preparation | Yes-or-no items with citations, and progress kept in the browser | | validator | Checking codes, tables or files | Text or a file, read in the browser and checked against bundled rules | | decision-tree | Eligibility and which clause applies | A short series of questions leading to a cited outcome | Every template produces plain files that run in the browser, with no server behind them and nothing loaded from elsewhere. Verifying. Shakedown runs five checks. A tool is not listed unless all five pass. 1. It works offline. The tool loads once and keeps working with the network disconnected. Every table and date it needs ships with it. 2. It cannot send anything. Every page carries a content security policy that includes connect-src 'self' and form-action 'none' , so the browser itself refuses any outside request. 3. It tracks nothing. No sign-in, analytics, cookies or counters. If the tool keeps work in the browser, it says so and offers a button to clear it. 4. Its answers match the worked examples. The tool is run against examples calculated by hand, including the awkward cases: zero, an empty file, a date that crosses a boundary. All test data is made up. 5. It shows its sources and its limits. Each result cites its regulation, paragraph and revision date. The tool says what it does not cover and that it is not professional advice, and carries an MIT license. Listing. Chartroom adds the verified tool to the catalog. It also handles the other outcomes: linking to an existing tool, merging an idea into another entry, and retiring a tool whose rule has been repealed.

title: Watching and routing
subtitle: The pipeline and its ten workers
summary: Tidegauge keeps the catalog accurate after a tool is published. On a schedule, it asks each official source whether anything has changed, using the cheapest che...
content: Watching and routing The pipeline and its ten workers Tidegauge keeps the catalog accurate after a tool is published. On a schedule, it asks each official source whether anything has changed, using the cheapest check that works: a header that says whether a file is newer, a structured feed, or a comparison of a page’s structure. | It watches | For | | --- | --- | | The Federal Register | New and proposed rules that touch the FAR, the DFARS or small business programs | | The eCFR | Changed clauses, thresholds and effective dates | | NIST’s publications | New revisions of standards such as SP 800-171 | | Tools the catalog links to | Dead links, a new paywall, tracking that was added | | Tools the project built | Whether each still matches the current rule | The monitor does not change a tool itself. It reopens the item so that the pipeline handles it: a live tool whose rule changed goes back to be rebuilt, or is retired if the rule was repealed. A parked idea is looked at again when the thing blocking it clears. A linked tool that breaks or starts tracking its users goes back to be reconsidered. Bellbuoy turns failures, paused items and approved edits into work for the right repository. Its main job is to avoid noise. If two hundred items fail on the same unfamiliar table, one task is opened, not two hundred: the worker builds a fingerprint from the worker’s name, the error code and the pattern of the failure, and adds to the count on an existing task when the fingerprint matches.

title: Why no worker uses AI
subtitle: The pipeline and its ten workers
summary: Many pipelines reach for an AI model when a page is messy. This one does not, anywhere. | | With an AI model at run time | With fixed rules | | --- | --- | --- ...
content: Why no worker uses AI The pipeline and its ten workers Many pipelines reach for an AI model when a page is messy. This one does not, anywhere. | | With an AI model at run time | With fixed rules | | --- | --- | --- | | Repeatability | The same input can give different answers | The same input gives the same output on any machine | | Explaining a result | Hard to say why a number was chosen | Every result traces to a line of code or a rule | | Cost | A charge for every page or item | None beyond the machine it runs on | | When confused | May invent an answer | Stops and waits for a rule | AI is used only while the rules are being written, under review. How AI is used has the detail.

title: Sub-tools: one rule for each case
subtitle: The pipeline and its ten workers
summary: Real pages do not look alike. One agency publishes a neat table and another buries the same figures in a brochure. Each variation is handled by a small, separat...
content: Sub-tools: one rule for each case The pipeline and its ten workers Real pages do not look alike. One agency publishes a neat table and another buries the same figures in a brochure. Each variation is handled by a small, separate rule called a sub-tool, kept in the repository of the worker that needs it, under tools// . A sub-tool has three parts: - A matching rule that says which pages or files it applies to. - The logic that extracts, scores or builds, written as plain code. - Fixtures : saved examples of the input together with the exact output expected, so that a test fails if the behaviour ever changes. When no sub-tool matches, the worker stops work on that one item and marks it needs subtool . Everything else in the queue carries on. Each awkward case is solved once and tested from then on.

title: How the workers stay in step
subtitle: The pipeline and its ten workers
summary: Workers do not talk to each other, and they do not touch the database. Each one asks a single service, Muster, for its next item, and reports the result back to...
content: How the workers stay in step The pipeline and its ten workers Workers do not talk to each other, and they do not touch the database. Each one asks a single service, Muster, for its next item, and reports the result back to it. - Leases. A worker claims an item for a limited time. If the worker stops, the lease runs out and the item is offered again. - One shared contract. The hub repository owns the definition of the handful of calls a worker makes ( lease , heartbeat , complete , fail , needs subtool ), the fourteen item states and the error codes. There is no separate shared-code repository for the ten workers to depend on. - Versions. Each worker states which version of the contract it speaks, and the hub checks every message against it. That lets one worker change and ship without the other nine being redeployed. - Three error codes. E TIMEOUT means something outside took too long. E PARSE means the data was broken. E NEEDS SUBTOOL means the data was valid and unfamiliar. - The wall is checked here too. The hub rejects any message to Moldloft that carries a raw page captured by Sextant. Cluster architecture describes the queue service and the database behind it.

title: Plainforge specification
subtitle: Platform · Section J.4
summary: Lightweight MIT-licensed Go Git server in the clearedstack namespace acting as cluster-primary source of truth with push-mirroring to GitHub.
content: Plainforge specification Lightweight MIT-licensed Go Git server in the clearedstack namespace acting as cluster-primary source of truth with push-mirroring to GitHub. components J.4 design formerly cs-git  Holds the primary copy of every repository, announces each change and mirrors code outward. Plainforge ( v0.1.0-draft , owned by Plainforge) is a clean-room, MIT-licensed Go Git server running in the clearedstack control-plane namespace. It replaces heavy third-party forges such as Forgejo—eliminating 40+ database tables and hundreds of megabytes of RAM—while serving as the cluster's primary source of truth for code and configuration. Overview & Role ClearedStack treats the cluster as primary and GitHub as the public mirror: - Headless Primary Git Server: Hosts bare .git repositories for clearedstack.com , all 10 deterministic workers (Trawl through Bellbuoy), sub-tools, and app.yaml

title: Failure Modes & Recovery
subtitle: Plainforge specification
summary: - GitHub Unreachable / Rate-Limited: Because Plainforge is primary, internal commits, Keelworks builds, and Shipkeeper deployments continue operating normally e...
content: Failure Modes & Recovery Plainforge specification - GitHub Unreachable / Rate-Limited: Because Plainforge is primary, internal commits, Keelworks builds, and Shipkeeper deployments continue operating normally even if outbound mirroring to GitHub is temporarily unreachable. - Build Loop Prevention: Digest updates written back by Keelworks to app.yaml are tagged [skip-ci] so Plainforge does not re-trigger an infinite build loop. - Volume Loss / Corruption: Plainforge holds one of the cluster's three Persistent Volume Claims. Nightly backups archive the bare repositories, encrypt them client-side with age , and transfer them off-node. The automated monthly restore drill mounts the restored bare repositories in an isolated scratch area and runs Git consistency checks to prove recoverability. - Pod Restart: High Priority Class protects Plainforge from eviction; on restart, k3s reattaches the PVC with all bare repositories intact.

title: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries
subtitle: Plainforge specification
summary: - ClusterIP Only: Plainforge has zero public Ingress and is unreachable from the open internet. Default-deny NetworkPolicy restricts cluster-internal access to ...
content: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries Plainforge specification - ClusterIP Only: Plainforge has zero public Ingress and is unreachable from the open internet. Default-deny NetworkPolicy restricts cluster-internal access to authorized control-plane peers. - No Unapproved Public Commits: Anonymous ✎ Edit proposals cannot reach Plainforge directly; they must pass the 5-layer anti-spam shield in Muster and explicit human approval in Countersign before Bellbuoy writes a commit. - Source-Only Public Mirror: Only source code commits and tags mirror to GitHub; signed OCI container images remain strictly internal inside Lazarette. - Clean-Room MIT Licensing: Written from scratch in Go under the MIT license, with no upstream forge license or dependency baggage. - Unprivileged Execution: Runs as non-root with dropped Linux capabilities and no privilege escalation.

title: Public edits and what stays private
subtitle: Platform · Section J.2
summary: How a reader is meant to propose a change without an account, the five checks that keep that safe, where each proposal goes, and the line between what the project shows and what it hides.
content: Public edits and what stays private How a reader is meant to propose a change without an account, the five checks that keep that safe, where each proposal goes, and the line between what the project shows and what it hides. cluster J.2 design  The design has no login anywhere. A reader should be able to see what the pipeline is doing, see what failed and why, and propose a fix, all without creating an account. This page describes how that is meant to work, and where the line sits between what is shown and what is hidden. This website is a set of plain files with nothing behind it, so there is nowhere for a proposal to go. The Edit button further down this page is a preview of the form. It sends nothing. To suggest a change today, open an issue on GitHub or write to contact@clearedstack.com. Why there is no lock Most projects hide th

title: Why there is no lock
subtitle: Public edits and what stays private
summary: Most projects hide their queues and their errors behind a sign-in, or a status page that says everything is fine. This design does the opposite, for a practical...
content: Why there is no lock Public edits and what stays private Most projects hide their queues and their errors behind a sign-in, or a status page that says everything is fine. This design does the opposite, for a practical reason: every curious reader is a possible tester. When a reader finds a case the pipeline has no rule for, that case becomes a tested rule, and the system is better for it. See Sub-tools.

title: Proposing an edit
subtitle: Public edits and what stays private
summary: Anything a reader might want to correct carries a small Edit button: a description, a setting, a rule. Pressing it opens a form showing what the element holds n...
content: Proposing an edit Public edits and what stays private Anything a reader might want to correct carries a small Edit button: a description, a setting, a rule. Pressing it opens a form showing what the element holds now, with room for the proposed change and the reason. The reader does not need to know which repository owns what. A public file in the hub repository, ownership map.json , records for every editable element which repository it belongs to, which file, and what kind of change it is. | Kind of edit | What it changes | What happens once the owner approves | | --- | --- | --- | | DATA | Catalog text, a description, a record | The record is updated and the change is logged | | CONFIG | A worker’s settings, a scoring weight, a rule’s options | A change is committed to the owning repository, tested, built and deployed | | ISSUE | A report of something broken, or a request for a missing rule | One task is opened in the owning repository, or added to an existing one for the same problem | After submitting, the button is meant to turn into a status label the reader can watch: Proposed , then Approved , Building and Live . A proposal that is declined changes nothing, and the decision is recorded. Preview · sends nothing Press the button to see the form a reader would fill in. Whatever you type stays in this page and is discarded when you close it.

title: Five checks instead of a login
subtitle: Public edits and what stays private
summary: Accepting proposals from anyone on the internet invites automated abuse. The design stops it without accounts and without an outside CAPTCHA service. | Check | ...
content: Five checks instead of a login Public edits and what stays private Accepting proposals from anyone on the internet invites automated abuse. The design stops it without accounts and without an outside CAPTCHA service. | Check | How it works | What it costs a real reader | | --- | --- | --- | | 1. Proof of work | On submit, the browser solves a small puzzle that takes about a second | Nothing noticeable. For a bot sending thousands, it is expensive | | 2. Honeypot | A field no person can see. Anything that fills it in is discarded | Nothing | | 3. Rate limit | Submissions are capped for each source address, using a one-way hash made with a secret that changes daily | Nothing. The address itself is never stored | | 4. Shape and size | The target must exist in ownership map.json , the proposal must be under 4 KB, and all markup and scripts are stripped | A long proposal has to be split | | 5. A person | Every proposal waits until the owner approves it | A wait | The fifth is the one that matters most. No proposal can reach a repository or the cluster by itself.

title: What is public and what is private
subtitle: Public edits and what stays private
summary: Being open about how the project works does not mean publishing a map of the machine it runs on. The rule is: hide the network, show the logic. | Public | Priva...
content: What is public and what is private Public edits and what stays private Being open about how the project works does not mean publishing a map of the machine it runs on. The rule is: hide the network, show the logic. | Public | Private | | --- | --- | | All source code, under the MIT license | Addresses, host names and names inside the cluster | | Every rule, scoring weight and tie-breaker | Network rules and the layout of the cluster | | Every sub-tool and its test examples | Database passwords, tokens and signing keys | | Health of each component, queue lengths and each item’s history | The secret used to hash visitor addresses | | Error codes such as E TIMEOUT , E PARSE and E NEEDS SUBTOOL | Visitor addresses, which are never stored | | Proposals and their status | The raw pages captured during observation | Four things in the design hold that line. - One door. Only the website can be reached from outside. The queue service, the database, the Git server, the registry and the workers have private addresses only. - Two namespaces. The control plane and the workers are separated, and each blocks traffic that is not explicitly allowed. - Views, not tables. The website reads the database through a restricted role that can see only views built for publication. A private column cannot appear on a page, because the website is never given it. - Errors are cleaned first. When something fails, the event Kubernetes produces often names a machine or an address. Shipkeeper removes those and maps the failure to one of the public error codes before anything is reported. A reader sees what broke and at which stage, not where. If a bad change does get through, the previous version is one step away: the last five signed images of every component are kept, and a rollback needs nothing from outside. See Cluster architecture.

title: What never to put in a proposal
subtitle: Public edits and what stays private
summary: A proposal is public by design. Do not include classified information, controlled unclassified information, export-controlled data, real contract figures or any...
content: What never to put in a proposal Public edits and what stays private A proposal is public by design. Do not include classified information, controlled unclassified information, export-controlled data, real contract figures or anything that identifies a real company’s bid. The same rule applies to an issue or an email. See What never goes in.

content: Overview & Role Sextant specification Sextant ( v0.1.0-draft ) is the deterministic observation worker in the ClearedStack v3.1 pipeline, replacing the original Stage 3 (Observe). Implemented as a Go service in the Sextant repository under the MIT License, it inspects public web pages, .gov portals, and agency PDFs using repeatable extractors and zero runtime AI. Its core responsibilities are: - Public-only inspection: Fetch open-web vendor marketing pages, government portals, and procurement PDFs without logging in, bypassing paywalls, or submitting forms. - Deterministic fact extraction: Produce strict, schema-validated JSON capturing a candidate tool's core job, inputs, outputs, login requirement, tracking profile, license or copyright, price model, cited public rule, observation date, and confidence tier ( Seen , Stated , or Unknown ). - Clean-room sealing: Seal all raw HTML, DOM snapshots, screenshots, and downloaded PDFs behind the clean-room wall so downstream specification and build workers (Waybill and Moldloft) never see vendor markup, stylesheets, or client-side scripts.

content: Interfaces & State Transitions Sextant specification Sextant communicates exclusively with Muster in the clearedstack namespace over cluster-private HTTP authenticated via its Kubernetes ServiceAccount ( CONTRACT VERSION=v1 ). It never connects directly to Logbook, Plainforge, or Lazarette. - Queue consumption: Polls Muster using lease , heartbeat , complete , fail , and needs subtool , draining priority lanes in strict order: urgent → normal → backfill . - Inbound states: - recorded — Newly deduplicated PA-XXXX candidates from Trawl. - observed (re-queued) — Items returned from needs subtool replay after a sub-tool fix ships, parked items whose blocker cleared in Tidegauge, or linked items flagged for drift. - Outbound transitions: - observed — Extraction succeeded; sanitized structured JSON facts are stored in core. and raw captures remain sealed behind the clean-room wall. - needs subtool — Fail-closed pause ( E NEEDS SUBTOOL ) when no registered sub-tool matches the target layout. - Spool durability: Extracted payloads are written to /var/spool/cs before acknowledging complete to Muster, preventing lost work during control-plane restarts.

title: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries
subtitle: Sextant specification
summary: - Passive public boundaries: Sextant never creates accounts, starts free trials, submits lead-capture forms, enters real contracting data, or circumvents paywal...
content: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries Sextant specification - Passive public boundaries: Sextant never creates accounts, starts free trials, submits lead-capture forms, enters real contracting data, or circumvents paywalls, robots.txt , or CAPTCHAs. If a tool sits behind a login or anti-bot gate, observation stops at the public surface and records vendor claims as Stated rather than Seen . - Strict clean-room wall: Raw HTML, DOM trees, stylesheets, client-side scripts, and binary PDFs are sealed at Sextant and never cross into Waybill or Moldloft. Muster enforces this contract boundary by rejecting any build payload containing raw observation artifacts. - Pod hardening & network policy: Runs as an unprivileged non-root user with dropped Linux capabilities, no privilege escalation, and a read-only root filesystem (writable only at /var/spool/cs ). Default-deny Kubernetes NetworkPolicy allows outbound HTTP/HTTPS for public fetches and cluster-private HTTP to Muster, while blocking direct access to Logbook, Plainforge, and Lazarette.

summary: Shakedown never connects directly to Logbook or holds database credentials. It polls Muster over cluster-private HTTP using its Kubernetes ServiceAccount identi...
content: Interfaces & State Transitions Shakedown specification Shakedown never connects directly to Logbook or holds database credentials. It polls Muster over cluster-private HTTP using its Kubernetes ServiceAccount identity ( lease , heartbeat , complete , fail , needs subtool ), always draining urgent before normal and normal before backfill . 1. Input state ( building ): Picks up items whose static bundle has been generated by Moldloft and compiled without Docker by Keelworks (using rootless BuildKit). 2. 5-condition verification suite: - Offline execution: Confirms the tool loads once and operates with the network disconnected, with all lookup tables, rates, and regulatory dates bundled inside the repository. - Strict Content Security Policy: Verifies connect-src 'self' , default-src 'self' , and form-action 'none' so the browser blocks any outbound data transfer or remote asset fetch. - Zero tracking or accounts: Confirms zero sign-in walls, analytics scripts, cookies, visitor counters, or third-party beacons, and verifies any local browser storage usage is disclosed with a clear-data control. - Worked-example assertions: Executes hand-calculated worked examples, boundary edge cases (zero values, empty inputs, date boundaries), and synthetic test fixtures. - Citations, scope limits, and MIT license: Checks that every calculation cites its official source (regulation, paragraph, revision date), states scope exclusions and a non-advice disclaimer, and includes an MIT LICENSE file. 3. Output transition: Stages the signed verification result in /var/spool/cs and reports completion to Muster, hand-off ready for Chartroom to transition building → live . If regulatory ambiguity blocks verification, the item moves to parked .

content: Interfaces & Data Contracts Shipkeeper specification Shipkeeper bridges Git state, OCI digests, Kubernetes workloads, and public Portal telemetry: - Desired State (Plainforge + Lazarette): Reads app.yaml definitions from Plainforge and verifies corresponding sha256 digests in Lazarette (up to 5 retained versions per app). - Cluster Reconciliation (Kubernetes API): Applies Deployment , Service , and NetworkPolicy manifests via Server-Side Apply across clearedstack and cs-workers . - 1-Click App Store Actions ( /platform/ registry via Muster): - Install: Applies an app's manifests into its target namespace for the first time. - Upgrade: Rolls the Deployment forward to the latest signed digest built by Keelworks. - Pause: Scales the workload down cleanly without deleting its configuration, PVC, or queue state. - Rollback: Switches app.yaml and the live Deployment back to one of the previous 5 signed digests retained in Lazarette. - Sanitized Telemetry (Shipkeeper -> Muster): Watches Kubernetes Pod , Deployment , and Event objects, strips internal metadata, and emits normalized health states ( healthy , idle , degraded , paused ) and standardized error codes ( E TIMEOUT , E PARSE , E NEEDS SUBTOOL ).

content: Interfaces & Data Contracts Trawl specification - Queue Lease Contract (Muster, CONTRACT VERSION=v1 ): Pulls work via lease , maintains progress with heartbeat , and reports outcomes via complete , fail , or needs subtool over cluster-private HTTP using its Kubernetes ServiceAccount identity. Workers always drain priority lanes in order: urgent -> normal -> backfill . - Deterministic URL Normalization: - Lowercases scheme ( https ) and hostname. - Strips tracking and session query parameters ( utm , ref , fbclid , gclid , session IDs) and fragments. - Removes redundant trailing slashes and default index filenames. - Enforces public-only scheme and host validation. - SHA-256 Deduplication & State Transitions: Computes the SHA-256 digest of the canonical URL and checks core. state via Muster: - Existing hash: Logs the sighting or mirror link against the existing PA-XXXX record without creating a duplicate. - New hash: Mints a persistent PA-XXXX ID (transitioning discovered -> recorded ) and queues the item for Sextant. - Local Spool ( /var/spool/cs ): Stages completed intake payloads locally before acknowledging to Muster; if the hub is restarting, spooled results are flushed in order on recovery.

content: Interfaces & State Transitions Waybill specification Waybill leases work from Muster in the clearedstack namespace over ServiceAccount-authenticated HTTP ( CONTRACT VERSION=v1 ), draining urgent → normal → backfill priority lanes. - Inbound state: approved (items approved for Build by the owner in Countersign, plus opt-out or factual correction requests routed through Countersign). - Processing steps: 1. Load the Countersign determination and official statutory citations (FAR, DFARS, NIST, eCFR). 2. Render the Go-template provenance block (or apply neutral phrasing if an opt-out is active). 3. Match the item to a tools/spec-profiles// sub-tool. 4. Compile the sanitized JSON build spec ( provenance , authority , schema , vectors ), resolving any conflict between vendor behavior and official government publications strictly in favor of the government text. - Outbound transitions: - building — Sanitized JSON build spec compiled and validated; item is ready for Moldloft. - needs subtool — Fail-closed pause ( E NEEDS SUBTOOL ) when no spec-profiles sub-tool matches the required tool structure. - Opt-out / correction updates on live tools trigger Chartroom republishing within the 5-day SLA.

content: Security & Clean-Room Boundaries Waybill specification - Enforces the clean-room wall before Moldloft: Waybill strips all raw HTML snapshots, vendor marketing URLs inside build inputs, vendor field labels, CSS classes, proprietary schemas, and scraped vendor test data. Only functional specifications anchored to official government publications and public worked examples cross into Moldloft. - Nominative attribution rules: Provenance notes never rate, criticize, or disparage observed products, and never imply vendor partnership, sponsorship, or endorsement. - Pod hardening & network policy: Runs non-root with dropped capabilities, read-only root filesystem (writable only at /var/spool/cs ), zero database credentials, and default-deny NetworkPolicy allowing only ServiceAccount HTTP to Muster.

content: Governing Regulations & Sources Acronym Table Builder Specification - FAR Part 15 & Section L Formatting Instructions: Many solicitations explicitly require an acronym list (either counted within or excluded from volume page limits) and require every acronym to be spelled out on first use. - Section L Precedence: Whether an acronym list belongs in front matter, an appendix, or inline only is governed by Section L ( Instructions, conditions, and notices to offerors ) or FAR Part 12 Instructions to Offerors . - Standard Federal & DoD Acronym Conventions: Bundles a read-only JSON dictionary of common public federal acquisition acronyms (e.g., FAR , DFARS , CLIN , COR , CO , PWS , SOW , SOO , RFP , RFQ , IFB , SAM , NAICS , PSC , CUI , NIST , CMMC , ATO , PoP ) strictly as suggested defaults that the user can accept, edit, or override.

title: Inputs, Processing Logic & Outputs
subtitle: Acronym Table Builder Specification
summary: Inputs | Field | Type | Constraints & Defaults | | --- | --- | --- | | draftText | Plain text or Markdown | Pasted volume text or local .txt / .md file read in ...
content: Inputs, Processing Logic & Outputs Acronym Table Builder Specification Inputs | Field | Type | Constraints & Defaults | | --- | --- | --- | | draftText | Plain text or Markdown | Pasted volume text or local .txt / .md file read in browser memory. | | existingAcronymList | Optional CSV/text pairs ( ACRONYM: Definition ) | Used to detect defined-but-unused acronyms and pre-fill known project-specific terms. | | minLength | Integer ( 2 – 5 ) | Defaults to 2 (minimum uppercase characters to treat as an acronym). | | ignoreCommonUnits | Boolean | Defaults to true (excludes units/identifiers like US , ID , PM , AM , GB , MB , PDF unless defined inline). | Deterministic Processing Logic 1. Inline definition detection: Scans for explicit expansion patterns in the draft: - Full Term Name (ACRONYM) — e.g., "Performance Work Statement (PWS)" - ACRONYM (Full Term Name) — e.g., "CUI (Controlled Unclassified Information)" 2. Standalone acronym extraction: Matches uppercase/alphanumeric tokens (e.g., FAR , CMMC , ISO , 800-171 excluded as pure numeric, DoD , FedRAMP via mixed-case allowlist) and records total occurrence count plus character/line index of first appearance . 3. First-use compliance check: Flags any acronym whose first appearance in draftText precedes its first inline expansion, or which appears without any inline expansion in the draft. 4. Collision & orphan detection: - Multi-meaning collision: Flags an acronym defined two different ways in the same draft (e.g., PO defined as both Project Officer and Purchase Order ). - Defined-but-unused orphan: Flags entries present in existingAcronymList that appear zero times in draftText . 5. Alphabetical normalization: Sorts unique acronyms case-insensitively ( A – Z ) and formats a clean two-column table ( Acronym , Definition ). Outputs - Acronym Definition Table: Sorted table with Acronym , Definition (editable inline), Occurrences , First Use Status ( Defined at first use | Defined late | Undefined ), and Flags ( Collision , Unused ). - QA Summary: Counts of unique acronyms, undefined acronyms, late-defined acronyms, collisions, and unused entries. - Local Exports: Markdown table, CSV, and plain-text tab-separated exports for direct paste into Word, LibreOffice, or Markdown proposal drafts.

content: Overview & Role Air-Gap Transfer Helpers Specification Air-Gap Transfer Helpers ( slug: air-gap-transfer-helpers , CLIN 0005 — Tactical & DevSecOps) is a client-side integrity and manifest utility in the ClearedStack catalog. Moving software, snapshot bundles, or compliance records onto a disconnected network requires proving three things at the boundary: every file is intact, no expected file went missing, and no extra file was introduced. Built directly around the two-sided workflow in Working on disconnected networks and Run it on a closed network, Air-Gap Transfer Helpers runs in the browser on both the sending side (outside) and receiving side (inside) without uploading a single byte over the network. It generates sorted sha256sum -compatible manifests ( payload.sha256 ), records transfer provenance metadata, and verifies received payloads with both hash comparison and file-count parity checks.

title: Governing Standards & Sources
subtitle: Air-Gap Transfer Helpers Specification
summary: | Component | Governing Standard / Reference | Rule Implemented | | --- | --- | --- | | Cryptographic Hash | NIST FIPS 180-4 ( Secure Hash Standard ) | SHA-256 ...
content: Governing Standards & Sources Air-Gap Transfer Helpers Specification | Component | Governing Standard / Reference | Rule Implemented | | --- | --- | --- | | Cryptographic Hash | NIST FIPS 180-4 ( Secure Hash Standard ) | SHA-256 (256-bit digest) computed via Web Crypto ( crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", ...) ). MD5 and SHA-1 are explicitly excluded due to collision vulnerabilities. | | Manifest Line Format | GNU Coreutils sha256sum / POSIX text format | \n (two-space separator), sorted lexicographically by UTF-8 byte order so browser output matches ( cd payload && find . -type f -print0 \| sort -z \| xargs -0 sha256sum ) . | | Transfer Provenance | ClearedStack Closed-Network Transfer Discipline (disconnected-networks, closed-networks) | Captures item name, version, source URL/commit, SHA-256 manifest digest, reviewer, transfer date, and replaced item; enforces file-count parity ( actualCount === manifestCount ). | Scope limits: Air-Gap Transfer Helpers verifies byte-level integrity and file-set completeness. As noted in Working on disconnected networks, a checksum proves a file has not changed since the checksum was made—it does not prove publisher identity unless the checksum is carried over an independent trusted channel or paired with a digital signature. This tool does not replace an organization's formal Cross-Domain Solution (CDS) or transfer approval policy.

title: Inputs, Processing Logic & Outputs
subtitle: Air-Gap Transfer Helpers Specification
summary: Inputs - Generate Mode (Sending / Outside Side): - Multi-file or directory selection ( or drag-and-drop). - Optional transfer record fields: preparer name, sour...
content: Inputs, Processing Logic & Outputs Air-Gap Transfer Helpers Specification Inputs - Generate Mode (Sending / Outside Side): - Multi-file or directory selection ( or drag-and-drop). - Optional transfer record fields: preparer name, source (URL, Git commit, or release tag), version, purpose, and replaced item. - Verify Mode (Receiving / Inside Side): - Received payload files or directory selection. - Carried payload.sha256 manifest file (uploaded or pasted). - Optional expected file count (if recorded separately out-of-band). Deterministic Browser-Only Processing Logic 1. Path normalization & deterministic sorting: Normalizes relative paths using forward slashes ( / ), strips any leading ./ or common root folder prefix consistently, and sorts entries lexicographically by code point (matching LC ALL=C sort ). 2. Client-side SHA-256 computation: Reads each File into memory as an ArrayBuffer (or processes large files in bounded chunks) and computes its SHA-256 digest via crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", ...) formatted as 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters. 3. Manifest generation (Generate Mode): - Emits payload.sha256 with one line per file. - Computes the SHA-256 digest of payload.sha256 itself so the manifest fingerprint can be read aloud or sent out-of-band. - Records totalFiles alongside the manifest. 4. Manifest verification & parity diff (Verify Mode): - Parses payload.sha256 strictly (each non-empty line must match ^[0-9a-f]{64} [ ].+$ ; malformed lines fail closed with E PARSE ). - Hashes every file in the received selection and partitions all paths into four disjoint sets: - OK : path in manifest and computed SHA-256 matches. - FAILED : path in manifest but computed SHA-256 differs. - MISSING : path in manifest but absent from received files. - EXTRA : path in received files but absent from manifest. - Evaluates countMatch = (receivedCount === manifestCount) and returns PASS if and only if FAILED.length === 0 , MISSING.length === 0 , EXTRA.length === 0 , and countMatch === true . 5. CLI command helper: Deterministically renders equivalent sha256sum , shasum -a 256 , PowerShell Get-FileHash , and ctr -n k8s.io images export/import commands for operators who also need terminal commands. Outputs - Generate Mode: Downloadable payload.sha256 file, manifest SHA-256 fingerprint, total file count, and a downloadable Markdown/JSON Transfer Record for approval paperwork. - Verify Mode: Clear PASS / FAIL verdict banner, counts for OK , FAILED , MISSING , and EXTRA , per-file status table, and an exportable verification log via Blob URL ( URL.createObjectURL ).

content: Overview & Role Certificate Verifier Specification Certificate Verifier ( slug: certificate-verifier , CLIN 0005 — Tactical & DevSecOps) is a client-side X.509 inspection and chain-verification tool in the ClearedStack catalog. On disconnected or air-gapped networks, browsers and operating systems cannot reach public OCSP responders, Authority Information Access (AIA) intermediate URLs, or NTP time servers. Internal enclaves also rely on private Certificate Authorities (CAs) that are not pre-installed in public trust stores, and host clocks can drift. Certificate Verifier lets operators decode PEM or DER certificates, inspect Subject Alternative Names (SANs) and key usages, validate signature chains against a user-supplied CA bundle, check expiry windows, and evaluate offline Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) entirely inside the browser—never transmitting certificates or private data off the machine.

title: Governing Standards & Sources
subtitle: Certificate Verifier Specification
summary: | Topic | Governing Standard | Scope in Tool | | --- | --- | --- | | Certificate & CRL Profile | RFC 5280 ( Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate...
content: Governing Standards & Sources Certificate Verifier Specification | Topic | Governing Standard | Scope in Tool | | --- | --- | --- | | Certificate & CRL Profile | RFC 5280 ( Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile ) | TBSCertificate , Subject , Issuer , Validity ( UTCTime / GeneralizedTime ), BasicConstraints ( cA , pathLenConstraint ), KeyUsage , ExtendedKeyUsage , SubjectAlternativeName , SKI / AKI , and X.509 v2 CRLs. | | ASN.1 Binary Encoding | ITU-T X.690 ( ASN.1 Distinguished Encoding Rules — DER ) | Deterministic tag-length-value (TLV) decoding of X.509 certificates and CRLs from raw bytes without external libraries making network calls. | | PEM Textual Encoding | RFC 7468 ( Textual Encodings of PKIX, PKCS, and CMS Structures ) | Parsing -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- and -----BEGIN X509 CRL----- blocks, including multi-certificate PEM bundles. | | Hashes & Signatures | NIST FIPS 180-4 ( SHA-256/384/512 ), RFC 8017 (RSA), RFC 5480 (ECDSA) | Fingerprinting and cryptographic signature verification via Web Crypto ( crypto.subtle.digest and crypto.subtle.verify ). | Scope limits: Certificate Verifier never requests or accepts private keys. It does not perform live OCSP or AIA network lookups, does not modify the host operating system's trust store, and does not replace formal PKI accreditation checks.

title: Inputs, Processing Logic & Outputs
subtitle: Certificate Verifier Specification
summary: Inputs - Target certificate: Pasted PEM text or uploaded .pem , .crt , .cer , or .der file (leaf or CA certificate). - Optional CA trust bundle: One or more PEM...
content: Inputs, Processing Logic & Outputs Certificate Verifier Specification Inputs - Target certificate: Pasted PEM text or uploaded .pem , .crt , .cer , or .der file (leaf or CA certificate). - Optional CA trust bundle: One or more PEM/DER intermediate and root CA certificates used as the local trust anchor set ( CAfile equivalent). - Optional offline CRL: A .crl file (PEM or DER) brought across the boundary on a schedule to check for revoked serial numbers. - Evaluation options: - Reference UTC timestamp: Defaults to the browser's current UTC time, with a manual override so operators can detect or compensate for disconnected clock drift. - Expiry warning window (seconds): Defaults to 2592000 seconds (30 days, matching openssl x509 -checkend 2592000 ). - Optional hostname: Checked against SubjectAlternativeName ( dNSName / iPAddress ). Deterministic Browser-Only Processing Logic 1. PEM/DER normalization: Detects RFC 7468 PEM headers or raw ASN.1 DER SEQUENCE ( 0x30 ) bytes. Extracts exact DER byte slices for the target certificate, each CA bundle certificate, and any supplied CRL. 2. SHA-256 fingerprint: Computes crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", derBytes) for each certificate. 3. ASN.1 DER decoding: Parses Certificate ( tbsCertificate raw slice, signatureAlgorithm OID, signatureValue bit string) and extracts Subject, Issuer, Serial Number, notBefore , notAfter , SubjectPublicKeyInfo , and standard X.509 v3 extensions ( BasicConstraints , KeyUsage , ExtendedKeyUsage , SubjectAlternativeName , SubjectKeyIdentifier , AuthorityKeyIdentifier ). 4. Chain construction & Web Crypto signature verification: - Builds the chain from leaf to a root in the supplied CA bundle by matching Issuer DN and AuthorityKeyIdentifier to Subject DN and SubjectKeyIdentifier . - Enforces BasicConstraints.cA === true and pathLenConstraint on every intermediate and root CA. - Verifies each child certificate's signature by calling crypto.subtle.importKey on the parent's SubjectPublicKeyInfo and crypto.subtle.verify over the child's exact tbsCertificate DER bytes (supporting RSA PKCS 1 v1.5, RSA-PSS, and ECDSA P-256 / P-384 with SHA-256/384/512). 5. Validity, SAN, & CRL evaluation: - Checks notBefore notAfter . - Matches optional hostname against SAN entries (supporting exact and single-label wildcard DNS rules). - If a CRL is supplied, verifies its signature against the matching issuer CA, checks whether the leaf serial number appears in revokedCertificates , and warns if evalTime > crl.nextUpdate (stale CRL). 6. Deterministic outcome classification: Maps failures to explicit diagnostics matching Working on disconnected networks: OK , Missing authority (unable to get local issuer certificate) , Expired or not yet valid (check clock drift) , Self-signed / untrusted root , Signature invalid , or Revoked in CRL . Outputs - Decoded certificate table: Subject, Issuer, Serial Number, Validity dates, SANs, Key Usage, Signature Algorithm, and SHA-256 fingerprint. - Chain verification diagram: Step-by-step link status from leaf through intermediates to root trust anchor. - Exportable verification record: JSON or Markdown report generated locally via Blob URL ( URL.createObjectURL ).

content: Worked Example & Verification Certificate Verifier Specification Synthetic Verification Case: 2-Certificate Internal Enclave Chain 1. Inputs: - Leaf: Synthetic ECDSA P-256 certificate for Subject: CN=server.internal.example , SAN: DNS:server.internal.example , Validity: 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z to 2027-01-01T00:00:00Z , BasicConstraints: cA=FALSE . - CA Bundle: Synthetic self-signed Internal Enclave Root CA ( BasicConstraints: cA=TRUE , KeyUsage: keyCertSign, cRLSign ). - Evaluation timestamp: 2026-11-15T00:00:00Z ; Warning window: 2592000 seconds (30 days); Hostname: server.internal.example . 2. Expected Processing & Output: - Signature check: crypto.subtle.verify confirms leaf tbsCertificate signature against Internal Enclave Root CA public key → VALID . - Validity check: 2026-11-15 is within [2026-01-01, 2027-01-01] → VALID . - 30-day expiry check: 2026-11-15 + 30 days = 2026-12-15 <= 2027-01-01 → PASS (47 days remaining). - SAN check: server.internal.example matches DNS:server.internal.example → MATCH . - Missing-CA negative test: Removing Internal Enclave Root CA from the CA bundle deterministically returns Missing authority (unable to get local issuer certificate) .

content: Overview & Role Compliance Matrix Generator Specification The Compliance Matrix Generator ( compliance-matrix-generator ) belongs to CLIN 0002 — Proposal & capture in src/data/catalog.ts . It transforms shredded solicitation requirements into a structured compliance matrix that cross-references Section L instructions, Section M evaluation factors, and Section C work requirements against the bidder's proposal outline, owners, and review status. content: Governing Regulations & Sources Compliance Matrix Generator Specification - FAR Part 15 & FAR 15.204-1 (Uniform Contract Format): Defines the structural separation between Section L ( Instructions, conditions, and notices to offerors ), Section M ( Evaluation factors for award ), and Section C ( Description/specifications/statement of work ). Where the FAR overhaul or FAR Part 12 commercial formats omit lettered sections, the tool maps Instructions to Offerors , Evaluation / Basis for Award , and SOW / PWS / SOO equivalently. - FAR 52.215-1 (Instructions to Offerors—Competitive Acquisition): Governs responsiveness to instructions, amendment acknowledgment, and compliance with solicitation-supplied templates. - Solicitation-supplied matrix rule: When a solicitation includes its own compliance matrix template or prescribes specific column headers (e.g., in Section L or a Section J attachment), the solicitation's columns take precedence over default columns.

summary: Inputs | Field | Type | Constraints & Defaults | | --- | --- | --- | | requirements | JSON/CSV from rfp-requirement-shredder or manual paste | Array of rows con...
content: Inputs, Processing Logic & Outputs Compliance Matrix Generator Specification Inputs | Field | Type | Constraints & Defaults | | --- | --- | --- | | requirements | JSON/CSV from rfp-requirement-shredder or manual paste | Array of rows containing id , source , text , and optional kind ( L , M , C , H , J ). | | proposalOutline | Structured list of volumes/sections | Each entry has volume , sectionNumber , heading , and optional pageLimit . | | crosswalkLinks | Array of { reqId, factorId, sectionId } | Links Section M evaluation factors to Section L instructions and Section C tasks. | | customColumns | Optional list of column names | Supports overriding default columns to match a government-mandated template. | Deterministic Processing Logic 1. Requirement ingestion & deduplication: Parses imported CSV/JSON or pasted rows, validates unique requirement IDs ( L-001 , M-001 , C-001 ), and preserves exact solicitation wording. 2. Three-way crosswalk validation: Checks alignment across the three requirement types: - Flags any Section M evaluation factor with no linked Section L instruction (orphan evaluation factor — candidate for a pre-award question to the contracting officer). - Flags any Section L content instruction with no linked Section M factor or Section C requirement. - Flags any requirement row whose Proposal location is unassigned or whose Status is not final when running the readiness check. 3. Outline-driven sorting: Orders matrix rows either by solicitation ID ( L → M → C ) or by proposal volume/section order so evaluators and red-team reviewers can walk the matrix top-to-bottom. 4. Status & coverage rollup: Computes deterministic counts by status ( Not started , Drafted , Reviewed , Final ), by owner, and by volume. Outputs - Interactive Compliance Matrix Table: Default columns per Answer every requirement: - ID - Source (section, paragraph, page) - Requirement (exact text) - Linked Factor / Instruction (crosswalk reference) - Proposal Location (volume, section, page) - Owner - Status ( Not started | Drafted | Reviewed | Final ) - Notes (open questions, assumptions, amendment references) - Gap & Orphan Report: Lists unmapped requirements, Section L/M mismatches, and incomplete rows. - Local Exports: Client-side CSV (RFC 4180 escaped) and JSON exports for spreadsheet or proposal-folder archiving.

content: Overview & Role CUI Marking Generator Specification The CUI Marking Generator ( slug: cui-marking-generator , CLIN 0003 — Cybersecurity & compliance, template family calculator ) is a static, browser-only utility that builds compliant banner lines, first-page Designation Indicator Blocks, and portion-marking legends for Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI). It prevents common marking mistakes—such as inventing categories, omitting Limited Dissemination Controls (LDCs), or applying retired legacy markings—by constraining selections to the bundled NARA CUI Registry. Scope boundaries: - Generates text markings for unclassified CUI only. - Does not cover classified information markings, ITAR/EAR export-control legends beyond CUI Specified categories, or agency-specific Security Classification Guides (SCGs) that supersede general marking rules. - Does not decide whether information qualifies as CUI; the contracting agency determines what is CUI under the contract.

content: Governing Regulations & Sources CUI Marking Generator Specification - 32 CFR Part 2002 ( Controlled Unclassified Information ), specifically § 2002.20 (Marking): Establishes government-wide CUI banner, designation indicator, portion marking, and legacy-marking retirement rules. - NARA CUI Registry (archives.gov/cui): Authoritative list of CUI Basic and CUI Specified categories, category markings, and Limited Dissemination Controls ( FEDCON , NOFORN , NOCON , DL ONLY , FED ONLY , REL TO , DISPLAY ONLY ). - DoD Instruction 5200.48 ( Controlled Unclassified Information ) and dodcui.mil marking guidance: Establishes Department of Defense practice requiring the CUI banner at both the top and bottom of every page and the standardized 5-line Designation Indicator Block.

title: Inputs, Processing Logic & Outputs
subtitle: CUI Marking Generator Specification
summary: Inputs - Marking profile: NARA Standard (32 CFR 2002) (top-of-page banner) or DoD (DoDI 5200.48) (top-and-bottom banner). - CUI Categories: Multi-select from th...
content: Inputs, Processing Logic & Outputs CUI Marking Generator Specification Inputs - Marking profile: NARA Standard (32 CFR 2002) (top-of-page banner) or DoD (DoDI 5200.48) (top-and-bottom banner). - CUI Categories: Multi-select from the bundled NARA CUI Registry lookup table (including category code, full name, and Basic vs Specified flag—e.g., CTI , EXPT , PRVCY , PROCURE , SSEL , PROPIN , CRIT ). - Limited Dissemination Controls (LDCs): Optional multi-select from the bundled NARA LDC table (e.g., FEDCON , NOFORN , NOCON , DL ONLY , REL TO [country list] ). - Designation Indicator fields: - controlledByAgency : Department, Agency, or DoD Component name - controlledByOffice : Optional originating office or program - poc : Point of contact name and phone number or email - decontrol : Optional decontrol date or event - Portion marking toggle: Boolean ( includePortionGuidance ) for (CUI) / (U) paragraph marking rules. Deterministic Processing Logic 1. Category & legacy validation: - Rejects any category code not present in the bundled NARA CUI Registry. - Detects and blocks retired legacy markings ( FOUO , For Official Use Only , SBU , LES ) with an explanatory notice citing 32 CFR § 2002.20. 2. Banner string construction: - Start with CUI . - If one or more CUI Specified categories are selected, append //SP-/ (category markings sorted deterministically). CUI Basic categories are recorded in the Designation Indicator Block rather than added to the banner unless required by agency policy. - If one or more LDCs are selected, append /// . - Example: CTI (Specified) + FEDCON → CUI//SP-CTI//FEDCON . - If only CUI Basic categories and no LDCs are selected → CUI . 3. Designation Indicator Block construction: - Formats the standardized block using the validated inputs: text Controlled by: Controlled by: CUI Category: Limited Dissemination Control: POC: - Appends Decontrol on: only when provided. 4. Portion marking rule: When enabled, emits (CUI) and (U) markers with the mandatory rule that if portion marking is used anywhere in a document, it must be applied throughout the entire document. Outputs - Banner line with placement guidance (top of every page for NARA; top and bottom of every page for DoD). - Copy-ready Designation Indicator Block . - Portion marking legend (when enabled) and compliance reminders (do not over-mark non-CUI; CUI remains CUI until formally decontrolled).

content: Overview & Role Indirect Rate Estimator Specification The Indirect Rate Estimator ( indirect-rate-estimator , CLIN 0001 : Pricing & cost accounting) is a standalone, MIT-licensed static browser utility generated by Moldloft using the deterministic calculator stack template. It takes a contractor's annual direct labor, indirect labor, and indirect cost pools (fringe, overhead, and G&A) and calculates the resulting indirect rates under selectable allocation base conventions. Because indirect rates are meaningless without their allocation bases, the tool enforces explicit base selection and displays the exact numerator and denominator for every rate. It executes 100% in browser memory with zero backend servers, zero runtime AI, and zero outbound network requests.

subtitle: Indirect Rate Estimator Specification
summary: Inputs | Field | Type | Constraints / Options | Default | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Direct Labor Dollars ( DL ) | Currency ( $ ) | >= 0.00 | 600,000.00 | | In...
content: Inputs, Calculation Logic & Outputs Indirect Rate Estimator Specification Inputs | Field | Type | Constraints / Options | Default | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Direct Labor Dollars ( DL ) | Currency ( $ ) | >= 0.00 | 600,000.00 | | Indirect Labor Dollars ( IL ) | Currency ( $ ) | >= 0.00 | 100,000.00 | | Fringe Pool ( P fringe ) | Currency ( $ ) | >= 0.00 (allowable fringe costs only) | 210,000.00 | | Overhead Pool ( P oh ) | Currency ( $ ) | >= 0.00 (allowable overhead costs only) | 156,000.00 | | Overhead Base Convention | Enum | dl plus fringe (direct labor + fringe on direct labor) or dl only (direct labor alone) | dl plus fringe | | G&A Pool ( P ga ) | Currency ( $ ) | >= 0.00 (allowable G&A costs only) | 112,320.00 | | G&A Base Convention | Enum | total cost input (all costs beneath G&A) or value added (excludes subcontracts & direct materials/ODCs) | total cost input | | Subcontracts & Direct Materials / ODCs ( Sub ODC ) | Currency ( $ ) | >= 0.00 (included in G&A base under total cost input , excluded under value added ) | 0.00 | Calculation Logic 1. Fringe Rate ( R fringe ): - fringe base = DL + IL - R fringe = P fringe / fringe base (expressed as % , 0.00% if fringe base == 0 ) 2. Fringe Allocated to Direct Labor ( F dl ): - F dl = DL R fringe 3. Overhead Base ( B oh ) & Overhead Rate ( R oh ): - If dl plus fringe : B oh = DL + F dl - If dl only : B oh = DL - R oh = P oh / B oh (expressed as % , 0.00% if B oh == 0 ) 4. G&A Base ( B ga ) & G&A Rate ( R ga ): - If total cost input : B ga = DL + F dl + P oh + Sub ODC - If value added : B ga = DL + F dl + P oh - R ga = P ga / B ga (expressed as % , 0.00% if B ga == 0 ) Outputs - Calculated Rates: Fringe Rate ( % ), Overhead Rate ( % ), and G&A Rate ( % ) rounded to 2 decimal places ( XX.XX% ), with full-precision ratios shown in the formula breakdown. - Pool-and-Base Breakdown Table: Shows each pool's numerator, exact denominator components, and resulting rate. - Unallowable Cost Reminder: Checklist reminding users to segregate unallowable expenses (FAR 31.205) into separate general-ledger accounts before entering pool totals. - Handoff Summary: Displays the three resulting rates formatted for direct entry into the Wrap Rate Calculator.

content: Overview & Role NAICS-to-PSC Crosswalk Specification naics-psc-crosswalk ( CLIN 0004 , category: "market" , slug: naics-psc-crosswalk ) is a static, browser-only market research utility in the ClearedStack catalog. Its job is to help contractors and buyers move deterministically between North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes (which describe what kind of business sells a capability) and Product and Service Codes (PSCs) (which describe what the government is buying on a contract action). As documented in Codes, registration and small business status, there is no official one-to-one mapping between NAICS and PSC: one NAICS code corresponds to many PSCs and vice versa. naics-psc-crosswalk therefore provides a deterministic, ranked starting point built from official taxonomy descriptions and historical federal award pairings, paired with an optional SBA size-standard check for the selected NAICS code.

content: Governing Regulations & Sources NAICS-to-PSC Crosswalk Specification Every code, description, and threshold bundled in naics-psc-crosswalk is derived from public federal sources: | Source | Authority / Scope | How Used in Tool | | --- | --- | --- | | OMB / U.S. Census Bureau NAICS | 2022 NAICS Manual (6-digit industry hierarchy) | Provides canonical 6-digit NAICS codes, titles, and sector prefixes (e.g., 54 Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services; 5415 Computer Systems Design). | | GSA / FPDS PSC Manual | Product and Service Code Manual (4-character codes) | Provides canonical 4-character PSCs and top-level classification: digit ( 0 – 9 ) = Products, A = Research & Development, other letters ( B – Z , e.g., D for IT, R for professional/management support) = Services. | | 13 CFR Part 121 | SBA Table of Size Standards | Supplies the small business size standard for each 6-digit NAICS code, measured either in average annual receipts (5-year average, mostly services) or number of employees (24-month average including part-time staff, mostly manufacturing and R&D). | | 13 CFR 121.103 & FAR Part 19 | Affiliation & solicitation-level NAICS assignment | Documents that affiliates count toward size and that the solicitation's assigned NAICS code controls size eligibility as of the offer submission date. |

title: Inputs, Processing Logic & Outputs
subtitle: NAICS-to-PSC Crosswalk Specification
summary: Inputs | Field | Type | Validation / Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | mode | Enum ( naics to psc \| psc to naics \| keyword ) | Selects lookup direction. | | query...
content: Inputs, Processing Logic & Outputs NAICS-to-PSC Crosswalk Specification Inputs | Field | Type | Validation / Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | mode | Enum ( naics to psc \| psc to naics \| keyword ) | Selects lookup direction. | | query | String | 2–6 digit NAICS prefix/code ( ^\d{2,6}$ ), 1–4 character PSC prefix/code ( ^[A-Z0-9]{1,4}$ ), or keyword tokens. | | psc category | Enum ( all \| products \| rd \| services ) | Optional filter based on first character of PSC ( 0-9 , A , B-Z ). | | size metric value | Number (optional, >= 0 ) | Optional user-entered 5-year average annual receipts (USD) or 24-month average employee count, including affiliates. | Deterministic Processing Logic 1. Input normalization: Trim whitespace, strip hyphens, uppercase PSC characters, and reject non-alphanumeric control characters. 2. Taxonomy lookup: - Exact 6-digit NAICS or 4-character PSC matches resolve directly against the bundled static JSON tables ( naics-2022.json , psc-manual.json ). - Shorter prefixes (2–5 digit NAICS or 1–3 character PSC) return all matching child codes sorted lexicographically. - Keyword queries run deterministic, case-insensitive token matching against official titles and descriptions. 3. Crosswalk ranking: For a selected NAICS (or PSC), query the bundled naics-psc-crosswalk.json index and sort paired codes deterministically by bundled co-occurrence tier ( Primary , Secondary , Related ), breaking ties lexicographically by code. 4. Optional size-standard evaluation: When size metric value is provided for a 6-digit NAICS code: - Compare size metric value Small (under NAICS ) - Compare size metric value > size standard limit -> Other than small (under NAICS ) - Always attach the effective table date and an affiliation reminder ( 13 CFR 121.103 ). Outputs - Primary code card: Code, official 2022 NAICS title (or PSC title and category), and SBA size standard ( measure , limit , effective date ). - Ranked crosswalk table: Paired PSCs (or NAICS codes) with category badge, official description, and match tier ( Primary / Secondary / Related ). - Size check result (if entered): Pass/exceed comparison against the NAICS size standard with explicit note that the solicitation's assigned NAICS code governs. - Exportable search summary: Plain-text, JSON, or CSV list of selected codes for use in SAM.gov or USASpending award searches.

content: Overview & Role NDC Eligibility Checker Specification ndc-eligibility-checker ( CLIN 0004 , category: "market" , slug: ndc-eligibility-checker ) is a static, browser-only decision tool in the ClearedStack catalog. It determines whether a business qualifies as a Nontraditional Defense Contractor (NDC) under federal defense acquisition statute and explains what contracting pathways that status opens up. No government agency issues a certificate for NDC status. As explained in Codes, registration and small business status, an offeror establishes its status by comparing its own Department of Defense (DoD) contract and subcontract history against the statutory definition and may be asked to represent that status in a solicitation response.
